The lifecycle

The journey shows eight stages (§1.1.1a). The master counts ten (§1.3): it treats keeping data and deleting it as stages of their own. Management runs alongside every other stage (§1.3).

AI across the lifecycle →

01

Generation

§2.0OverviewStandardExpert
You are here

Data is created by systems, devices, people or algorithms before any later step can begin, whether or not anyone notices. §2.0

In the journey · Stage 1Watch this stage

Where data is born.

Systems, devices, people and algorithms make data before anything else can happen. The rules come first: what it is for, who agreed, how it is handled — and only what is needed. At Tamsworth Health, it is a bedside monitor.

What

A reading is created

A machine makes this data: the monitor measures a patient. Each reading is an event that records a change. One row of data now exists.

Tools: Bedside patient monitors that feed a hospital's record system. Tamsworth uses Philips IntelliVue monitors and Epic.

Owner: IT

How

One row, ten fields

The reading is written in one agreed shape: the same ten fields, every time.

Tools: A health-data standard for the row's shape. Tamsworth uses HL7 FHIR (Observation).

Owner: Data engineers

Why

Everything starts here

Every later stage trusts this row, so it is tagged at the source. Five fields name the patient, so they are flagged as sensitive at once.

Owner: Data engineers

When

Every 15 minutes

Every patient, around the clock.

Owner: Data engineers

Next

Collection

The row is ready for Stage 2 to pick up.

Tools: A streaming platform that carries rows on to collection, such as Apache Kafka.

Owner: Data engineers

With AIAct 2 · from the AI research file, not the master

Where AI can take the load

At the start of the lifecycle, AI can do the routine first round: find new data, describe it and tag it as it arrives. A person confirms what matters.

Why

What is recorded at the start travels with the data. DataHub puts it plainly: every later stage either inherits what was recorded or works around what was missed.

How

AI can be confidently wrong, so each automated step needs a review point that matches its risk.

Know which steps follow fixed rules and which are left to an AI agent to decide.

A good first pilot is high-volume, repetitive intake work with a baseline you can measure against.

Plan for the data AI makes itself. Prompts, answers, feedback and test runs are data too, and they flow back into the same systems, so the lifecycle becomes a loop.

§2.1

Where data comes from

You are hereStandard
  • §2.1.1
    Machines and systems

    Sensors, cameras and GPS devices, mobile apps, system logs, event streams, and algorithms or models all make data. Generative models can make synthetic data for testing where real data raises privacy or compliance concerns. §2.1.1

  • §2.1.2
    People

    People make data through forms, surveys, transactions and every interaction with an organization, its customers and third parties. §2.1.2

  • §2.1.3
    Forms of data

    Data comes structured (tables with a set schema), unstructured (images, video, email, text) or semi-structured (a mix, such as JSON or XML). §2.1.3a

  • §2.1.4
    Events

    Each data point can be an event: a record that something changed in the system that made it. §2.1.4

Who

Data engineers build the processes that make data; IT keeps the systems behind them running. §2.1.5a

Two sources, Varonis and Splunk, name no role for creation. §2.1.5a

Rules

Data is collected in standard formats, and personal data is handled under privacy rules. §2.1.5b

Where generated data carries a privacy risk, it can be anonymized or replaced with synthetic data. §2.1.5b

Retention needs are first asked for when a new source is brought on. §2.1.5b

Tools

One source describes AI agents that watch new data against governance policies and flag problems early. §2.1.5c

No tools are named beyond example source systems: point-of-sale systems, online shopping carts and feedback forms. §2.1.5c

What breaks

The named risk is privacy and compliance exposure at the moment data is made. §2.1.5d

No metrics are stated in the sources. §2.1.5d

With AIAct 2 · from the AI research file, not the master

Where AI can take the load

AI agents can keep scanning cloud, on-premises and software-as-a-service systems for new sources of data, and profile each new table as it appears.

Why

You cannot manage data you do not know exists. Informatica says finding each new source by hand takes weeks of IT effort, and that untracked "shadow" data is a security and compliance risk.

How

Let profiling run on its own. Kanerika says the data owner should still confirm what discovery finds.

Keep discovery running. Informatica warns that shadow data stays invisible unless it does.

§2.2

Capture at the source

You are hereStandard
  • §2.2.1
    Ways data is captured

    Data is acquired from outside organizations, typed in by hand inside the organization, or made by devices and systems. §2.2.1

  • §2.2.2
    Capturing changes

    Change data capture sends each insert, update and delete in a database on as an event, in real time. It is covered under collection. §2.2.2

Who

Not stated in the master’s sources. §2.2.3a

Rules

Not stated in the master’s sources. §2.2.3b

Tools

Not stated in the master’s sources. §2.2.3c

What breaks

Not stated in the master’s sources. §2.2.3d

§2.3

Design and inventory at creation

You are hereStandard
  • §2.3.1
    Judge before collecting

    Collecting everything is not needed. New data is judged first for quality and business relevance, from an inventory of what will be collected, how much, how sensitive it is and which rules apply. §2.3.1

  • §2.3.2
    Tag at the source

    Data is tagged by origin, purpose, sensitivity, source and how far it can be trusted. Personal and sensitive fields are flagged at once for masking and encryption. §2.3.2b

  • §2.3.3
    Where new data comes from

    Sources named include apps, devices and sensors, forms and surveys, APIs, transactional systems, emails, machine logs, partner uploads and licensed third-party data. §2.3.3

Who

Ownership of each dataset is assessed in the audit, and stewardship is set in the data management plan. §2.3.4a

Other roles at creation are not stated in these sources. §2.3.4a

Rules

Data is classified by sensitivity and regulatory need before it is collected, with handling guidelines for each type. §2.3.4b

Tools

Automated validation checks and standard formats where data comes in. §2.3.4c

One retailer example tags each online order with a customer ID, its source, the time and a flag for personal data. §2.3.4c

What breaks

Data that comes in unchecked or untagged weakens storage, access, analysis and security. One source says most quality problems start here. §2.3.4d

Collecting data that is not needed creates liability. §2.3.4d

With AIAct 2 · from the AI research file, not the master

Where AI can take the load

AI can record a new dataset's source, owner, shape and sensitivity as it lands, and classify it from day one. Generative AI can also write the field descriptions people find hard to supply.

Why

That context is easy to know on arrival and costly to rebuild later, when the people who remember it may have moved on.

How

Check every new source for quality and relevance before it comes in, and check again over time, because sources get worse.

AI suggests a sensitivity tag such as personal data, and a privacy lead confirms it. Tags the AI is unsure of go to a steward before they are published.

§2.4

Purpose, consent and planning before data exists

You are hereStandard
  • §2.4.1
    The planning step

    Before capture, goals, formats and definitions are set, the rules that apply are found, and privacy, security and handling rules are written to match. GDPR data minimization limits how much is captured and how long it is kept. §2.4.1

  • §2.4.2
    Plan from business goals

    Start from the business goal and map the data it needs. Some funders and regulators require a data management plan, which sets handling, ownership and quality rules and limits unneeded data. §2.4.2

  • §2.4.3
    Purpose and consent

    Say why the data exists, confirm it is needed, find the permission or consent that applies, and name the system that holds the official record. Personal or sensitive data needs permission or consent. §2.4.3

  • §2.4.4
    Questions a mature program answers

    Why the data exists, what it holds, who owns it, who can reach it, how long to keep it, whether a legal hold applies, whether it still has value, whether AI should use it, when to cut or delete it, and how to prove the rules worked. §2.4.4

  • §2.4.5
    Collecting too much

    Collecting too broadly can breach HIPAA, GDPR, PCI DSS and CMMC, and a bigger collection means a bigger breach. The control is an inventory of data types and where they live. §2.4.5

Who

Not stated for planning in the main planning source. Data management plans set ownership rules, and owners and stewards are named in general under governance. §2.4.6a

Rules

GDPR data minimization; exposure under HIPAA, GDPR, PCI DSS and CMMC; checks for consent and permission. §2.4.6b

Tools

Not stated in the master’s sources. §2.4.6c

What breaks

The named failure is collecting data with no plan for how long to keep it or when to delete it. §2.4.6d

With AIAct 2 · from the AI research file, not the master

Where AI can take the load

AvePoint says its AI can draft lifecycle policies from a plain-language request, with classification terms and retention rules suited to the industry and region.

Why

AvePoint claims this cuts weeks of regulatory research and workshops down to minutes.

How

A person stays firmly in control of what an AI-drafted policy actually does, and tailors its terms and rules to their own scope.

Collect on purpose and with consent. Be clear what the AI is for, keep personal data to a minimum, and check inputs where they are made.

Sources differ on where to start. Agility at Scale says set the rules for keeping and disposing of data first; Kanerika says start by profiling what the data holds.

02

Collection

§3.0OverviewStandardExpert
You are here

Collection selects the generated data that matters and brings it from its sources, such as databases, APIs and files, into the system. §3.0

In the journey · Stage 2Watch this stage

Where data is gathered.

Collection brings in the data that matters, without losing any. Each row is checked as it arrives, and sensitive fields travel encrypted. Tamsworth flags rows in doubt but never changes them. All land in Bronze, its raw copy.

What

Gather from many places

Tamsworth needs vitals, lab results and patient feedback together. Business stakeholders confirm what is needed; data engineers connect each source.

Tools: Interfaces to each source system. Tamsworth uses HL7 FHIR for its EHR, HL7 messages from its lab system, and Qualtrics for its survey.

Owner: Business stakeholders, Data engineers

How

Read, then keep side by side

Each source is read in its own format and loaded as it is. The three parts sit side by side for the same patient and time; joining them is processing's work.

Tools: Connectors that read each source and land it unchanged, such as Kafka Connect.

Owner: Data engineers

Why

Nothing may be lost

Data can be lost here: through overload, rows that arrive late or out of order, and poor inputs. Tamsworth checks four things as rows arrive: volume, velocity, variety and veracity.

Tools: A streaming platform that carries rows in, such as Apache Kafka, with tools that find and handle errors, such as Apache NiFi.

Owner: Data engineers

When

Every 15 minutes, as received

At Tamsworth, 80 monitored beds are read every 15 minutes: 7,680 vitals rows a day. Every part lands unchanged in Bronze, a raw copy that can be replayed.

Tools: Tamsworth keeps Bronze in Delta Lake.

Owner: Data engineers

Next

Processing

Stage 3 cleans and standardizes the raw row. Collection never edits it.

Tools: Processing tools that read from Bronze, such as Apache Spark or dbt.

Owner: Data engineers

With AIAct 2 · from the AI research file, not the master

Where AI can take the load

AI can take over much of the routine work of bringing data in: reading new formats, suggesting how fields map, and building connectors for new sources.

Why

Bringing in a new source has been slow, manual work: parsing formats, handling errors and fitting standards. Fivetran calls the old way workable, but slow and labor-intensive.

AngelHack reports that Discover Financial Services cut its pipeline build time from 30 days to about 15 minutes, saving roughly 200,000 hours. AngelHack does not name the platform; another source names Discover as an Alation customer.

How

Decide first how far to go: let AI help inside the pipeline you have, or let it build and run the pipeline itself.

The research found no source that places a human review step inside automated routing or connector building.

Collection can become a loop with the model: collect, train, test, then collect more where the model needs it. Volvo Cars does this with its vehicles' sensors, and every data point is collected with customer consent.

§3.1

How data is collected, and planning it

You are hereStandard
  • §3.1.1
    Ways to collect

    Data is collected through forms, surveys, interviews and observation; through APIs, databases, IoT sensors and web scraping; and from transactions, social media and manual entry. §3.1.1

  • §3.1.2
    Plan first

    Start with a plan to capture the data the work critically needs; capturing everything is common but weaker. Define the purpose, classify the data and drop redundant data at collection. §3.1.2

  • §3.1.3
    Request, then define

    In Splunk's lifecycle, data is requested on a template that records the source, its location, access, retention needs and expected volume. It is then defined: timestamps, intended use, sensitivity and the fields to extract. §3.1.3

Who

Business stakeholders confirm the needed data is collected; data engineers bring the sources into central databases. One source says the data team decides what to collect. §3.1.4a

Rules

Collection policies for each type of data, such as employee, partner and accounting data, and personal-data policies under privacy regulations. §3.1.4b

Retention needs are recorded when data is requested. §3.1.4b

Tools

One source says AI automates extraction from APIs, software services and unstructured inputs, with filtering, classification and removal of duplicates, and that agentic AI can decide what data it needs and run the collection. §3.1.4c

Also named: web scraping tools, e-commerce platforms, IoT sensors and APIs. §3.1.4c

What breaks

Data loss, and inputs that are irrelevant or of low quality. Inaccurate data weakens analysis. §3.1.4d

One measure is named: the estimated data volume on each request, in Splunk. §3.1.4d

With AIAct 2 · from the AI research file, not the master

Where AI can take the load

AI can gather data from many kinds of source, such as APIs, devices and business systems, and classify it, without a custom pipeline for each one.

Why

More data is not always better. Alwin Bakkenes of Volvo Cars says curation decides what a model needs, so that training is more efficient.

How

Before AI collects anything, a person decides how much automation the organization accepts: start in one area, or automate fully from the start.

Record where each dataset came from, so it can be audited, governed and reused safely.

§3.2

How data is brought in

You are hereStandard
  • §3.2.1
    Push and pull

    A source can write data to its target (push), or the data can be fetched from the source (pull). One source calls the line quite blurry: across a pipeline, data is both pushed and pulled. §3.2.1

  • §3.2.2
    Integration styles

    Extract, transform, load (ETL) changes data before it lands. Extract, load, transform (ELT) lands it first and changes it inside the warehouse. Federation reads across systems without moving data. Turning many sources into one format is slow, costly work. §3.2.2

  • §3.2.3
    Ingestion patterns

    Named patterns: one extractor for many source types, a converter between protocols, delivery to many destinations, transforming just before the data is needed, and real-time streaming. §3.2.3

  • §3.2.4
    Ingestion modes

    A pipeline takes data as a continuous stream, when an event triggers it, or in batches of a set size, and may set its own pace to suit what comes after it. §3.2.4

Who

Redpanda frames these as data engineering decisions. No further role is named for ingestion. §3.2.5a

Rules

A stated best practice: read data with flexible, self-describing formats such as JSON and CSV, so a change of format can be handled. §3.2.5b

Tools

Ingestion tools usually support ETL, and offer removal of duplicates, detection of a source's shape, and error handling. The tools themselves are under tools and connectors, and real-time ingestion. §3.2.5c

What breaks

To avoid bottlenecks, split the data into subsets processed in parallel, and balance the load across machines. §3.2.5d

With AIAct 2 · from the AI research file, not the master

Where AI can take the load

AI can recognize the shape of raw files such as JSON, XML and PDFs, work out what each field means, and suggest how it maps to fields already known.

Why

Kanerika says a mapping suggestion saves hours per source.

How

Suggest, review, then lock: AI proposes a mapping, a person approves it before production, and the mapping goes under version control.

Validate again at load time; it catches what a mapping review misses. A wrong mapping silently corrupts every table downstream.

Sources disagree on whether to bring data together in one place or query it where it sits. This research does not choose, and neither does the master.

§3.3

Tools and connectors

You are hereStandard
  • §3.3.1
    Redpanda

    A streaming platform compatible with Apache Kafka, with a built-in schema registry, web proxy and message broker. Producers write to topics and consumers read from them. §3.3.1

  • §3.3.2
    Kafka Connect

    Connects Kafka to other systems through declared connectors. Source connectors pull from databases, message brokers and app servers into topics; sink connectors push topic data on to indexes, batch systems or databases. §3.3.2

  • §3.3.3
    Debezium

    An open-source change data capture platform built on Kafka. It reads row-level changes from a database's transaction log, and usually runs through Kafka Connect. §3.3.3

  • §3.3.4
    Redpanda Connect change-capture inputs

    Eight certified inputs, among them PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, SQL Server and Oracle, run as one program with no Java runtime. Debezium, by comparison, runs on Java and usually needs Kafka Connect. §3.3.4

  • §3.3.5
    Other ingestion technologies

    Also named for ingestion: AWS IoT, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, Apache Kafka and Redpanda. §3.3.5

Who

Data engineers. Not stated further. §3.3.6a

Rules

Not stated in the master’s sources. §3.3.6b

Tools

Declared source and sink connectors. The source gives an example Debezium setup for MySQL. §3.3.6c

What breaks

Not stated in the sources, beyond the extra infrastructure Debezium needs: Java and Kafka Connect. §3.3.6d

§3.4

Real-time (streaming) ingestion

You are hereStandard
  • §3.4.1
    What it is

    Streaming collects data as it is created and makes it available soon after. Batch lets data pile up and handles it in chunks, at intervals from hours to months. §3.4.1

  • §3.4.2
    Streaming architecture

    A kind of event-driven design. Ingestion tools collect and pass on data in real time, holding messages in a log that is only ever added to; stream processors read it and send results to storage, alerts, dashboards or other services. §3.4.2

  • §3.4.3
    Five layers

    A streaming pipeline has five layers: the source, ingestion, temporary storage, processing, and the destination. §3.4.3

  • §3.4.4
    Pull, push or both

    The pipeline can query its sources on a schedule (pull), the sources can send data in (push), or one pipeline can do both. §3.4.4

  • §3.4.5
    What to plan for

    Volume, retention, freshness, availability and security. Redpanda's guidance is to aim at 80% of a cluster's sustained throughput, and its default is to keep messages for 24 hours. Freshness should match the decisions that use the data, and sensitive data needs encryption end to end, with GDPR named. §3.4.5

  • §3.4.6
    Delivery guarantees

    Kafka can deliver each message at least once (duplicates possible), exactly once, or at most once (losses possible, never duplicates). Each trades speed against reliability. §3.4.6a

Who

Not stated in the master’s sources. §3.4.7a

Rules

Encrypt data in transit and at rest; comply with GDPR, HIPAA and industry rules; control access to sensitive data by role. §3.4.7b

Choose batch or real time by use case, comparing the return on each. §3.4.7b

Tools

Backpressure matches the rate of intake to what processing can handle. Retries improve delivery but may slow throughput. Apache NiFi and built-in mechanisms find and handle errors. Throughput and delay are watched all the time. §3.4.7c

What breaks

Data lost to overload when there is no backpressure; events that arrive out of order (handled by watermarking); disks filling from retained logs, causing slowdowns and cost; and data that grows unexpectedly. §3.4.7d

With AIAct 2 · from the AI research file, not the master

Where AI can take the load

During streaming, AI can shift computing resources as the load changes and watch performance, to keep delays short for critical work.

Why

Companies want answers in milliseconds, not after hours of batch processing, and live AI applications need data that is kept up to date.

How

Predictive models can spot inconsistencies, anomalies and duplicates as data comes in.

Plan for change: pipelines break when a source changes its shape.

§3.5

Change data capture

You are hereStandard
  • §3.5.1
    What it is for

    Change data capture keeps systems consistent by sending each change in an operational database on as an event, in real time. A framework between source and destination lets each work at its own pace. §3.5.1

  • §3.5.2
    Push-based

    The source does the work: a trigger runs on each change and tells the framework. Simple, but many triggers slow the source's writes, and adding them changes its schema. §3.5.2a

  • §3.5.3
    Pull-based

    The framework finds the changes: by querying for a last-modified time (simple, but it loads the source and handles deletes poorly), or by reading the database's log (the lowest load, but log formats differ and need other tools to read). §3.5.3

  • §3.5.4
    Reference architecture

    A connector at the source, a buffer or queue that absorbs changes in the flow, and a connector at the destination that writes the changes on. §3.5.4

  • §3.5.5
    Where it is used

    Copying to a warehouse so analysis does not slow the live system; moving to the cloud; linking microservices; keeping caches and indexes current; live reports; and audit logs for compliance in banking and healthcare. §3.5.5

Who

Not stated in the master’s sources. §3.5.6a

Rules

Audit logs of change events, kept to prove compliance. §3.5.6b

Tools

Read the log for customer-facing databases and critical write paths; use triggers where write speed matters less, and queries only where log reading is not supported. Use mature tools, and put a buffer in the middle. §3.5.6c

What breaks

Slower writes at the source (triggers), extra read load (queries), and log formats that differ (log reading). Schema changes, delivery guarantees, security and monitoring are not covered. §3.5.6d

§3.6

Event streaming

You are hereStandard
  • §3.6.1
    The core model

    Events flow one way, continuously, from producers that make them to consumers that act on them. §3.6.1

  • §3.6.2
    Patterns

    Publish and subscribe, through a broker; event sourcing, where a system's state is kept as its events and rebuilt by replaying them; separate models for writing and for reading; and replaying past events to test or to fill a new feature. §3.6.2

  • §3.6.3
    Design choices

    Processing can keep context across events, as fraud and anomaly detection do, or treat each event alone. It can run in sequence (strict, but it can bottleneck) or in parallel (faster, but harder to coordinate). §3.6.3

  • §3.6.4
    Streaming or batch

    Choose by how fresh the data must be, the resources at hand (batch is easier to plan), consistency and complexity. Micro-batching, small batches every few milliseconds to minutes, sits between; Apache Spark and Apache Flink support it. §3.6.4

Who

Not stated in the master’s sources. §3.6.5a

Rules

Not stated in the master’s sources. §3.6.5b

Tools

Message queues and streaming platforms. The source gives a RabbitMQ example. §3.6.5c

What breaks

Near-simultaneous changes can conflict, and streaming is harder to design and maintain than batch. Brokers, partitions, retention, schema registries, security, governance and failure modes are not covered. §3.6.5d

§3.7

Ingestion methods and governance

You are hereStandard
  • §3.7.1
    Three ways in

    Data is entered or created (support tickets, sensors, web forms), acquired from third parties under sharing agreements, or captured from automated streams such as equipment and point-of-sale systems. §3.7.1

  • §3.7.2
    Practices at ingestion

    Automated validation checks, standard formats and documented metadata. One source says to validate and cleanse at capture, removing errors, duplicates and non-standard entries. §3.7.2

  • §3.7.3
    The catalog at ingestion

    A central record of sources, lineage and quality measures. §3.7.3

  • §3.7.4
    Integrations and APIs

    Integrations and APIs are the means of capture. §3.7.4

Who

Not stated, beyond business and data owners being asked to set policy. §3.7.5a

Rules

Sharing agreements for data acquired from third parties; licensing and sharing limits set in the data management plan. §3.7.5b

Tools

Automated validation, and the catalog as the central record. Atlan says its Context Agents draft descriptions, tags and quality notes automatically. §3.7.5c

What breaks

The catalog tracks quality measures at the source. §3.7.5d

With AIAct 2 · from the AI research file, not the master

Where AI can take the load

AI can turn unstructured intake, such as scanned forms, invoices and contracts, into structured records.

Why

Scripts and older robotic process automation break when an input changes, such as a new invoice layout or a renamed column. AI steps read the input and adapt, so more of intake can be automated.

How

Most enterprise data is not structured, and each format needs its own treatment: text needs language processing, images need recognition models, audio needs transcription.

AWS says ingestion for generative AI keeps documents, transcripts and images in their native formats, and must keep picking up changes and deletions as well as new items.

Unstructured data is rarely governed as carefully as structured data, and generative AI makes it a main input. It needs the same management and governance at every step.

Lineage starts at the original source and runs through ingestion, third-party and synthetic data included.

§3.8

Collection in customer-data and pipeline terms

You are hereStandard
  • §3.8.1
    Collection methods

    Tracking on websites and apps (scripts, SDKs, pixels); API connections to payment, CRM and marketing tools; system logs; and manual entry on forms with validation. §3.8.1

  • §3.8.2
    Batch or real time

    Batch suits large or historical transfers, often run off-peak. RudderStack describes real-time collection with privacy controls, schema validation, consent management and audit logging. §3.8.2

  • §3.8.3
    By hand or automated

    Validation can be checked by hand now and then, or run on every record as it is collected. §3.8.3

  • §3.8.4
    Where data is made and captured

    Sources named: employee reports, emails and documents; sensors and equipment; website behavior; billing software; and cloud platforms. §3.8.4

  • §3.8.5
    Where data is made and collected

    User input, applications and automated processes, and outside sources such as devices, web forms, partners and third-party services. Incoming data is checked for quality and relevance before production use. §3.8.5

Who

Not stated in the master’s sources. §3.8.6a

Rules

Consent management and privacy controls at collection (vendor features), and an inventory of data types and where they are. §3.8.6b

Tools

SDKs, pixels, REST or GraphQL APIs, and scheduled pipeline syncs. The streaming and change-capture tools under §3.3 to §3.5 remain the infrastructure. §3.8.6c

What breaks

RudderStack says checking by hand risks oversights that real-time validation at collection prevents. It states no measure. §3.8.6d

03

Processing

§4.0OverviewStandardExpert
You are here

Processing turns collected data into a usable form: it integrates, cleanses and checks the data so it can be prepared for analysis. §4.0

In the journey · Stage 3Watch this stage

Where data is prepared.

Processing makes collected data trustworthy and usable. Tamsworth cleans, reshapes, joins and trims the three parts from Bronze into one row, then tests it. A row that passes becomes Silver; one that fails waits for a person.

What

Make the raw parts trustworthy

Five steps turn the parts in Bronze into one row that can be trusted: clean, reshape, join, trim, then test. Data engineers build the pipelines; data scientists explore the raw data first, to find what is useful.

Tools: Pipeline and transformation tools. Tamsworth uses Apache Spark for its pipelines and Jupyter notebooks for exploring.

Owner: Data engineers, Data scientists

How

Clean, reshape, join, trim

Remove repeats and errors, put dates in one form, join the three parts on patient ID and time, and drop fields nobody uses. Tamsworth keeps its late part and lines it up with its patient when it joins.

Tools: Transformation tools that run on a cluster or in the warehouse, such as Apache Spark or dbt, scheduled and watched by Apache Airflow.

Owner: Data engineers

Why

Later stages depend on this one

Dashboards and models rely on consistent processing, and logic nobody documented spreads its errors. At Tamsworth, preparing data takes most of the data team's time.

Owner: Data engineers

When

Last, a quality gate

Tamsworth tests every row before it moves on. A row that passes becomes Silver. A row that fails goes to a repair queue, where a person looks at it.

Tools: Data quality tools that write and run tests, such as Great Expectations, scheduled by Apache Airflow.

Owner: Data engineers, A person

Next

Storage

Stage 4 keeps the Silver row beside Bronze. Tamsworth makes Gold, a business-ready table built for one question, from Silver later, in Stage 6.

Tools: A data lake or a cloud warehouse such as Snowflake.

Owner: Database administrators

Where AI can take the load

AI can take over much of the routine work of preparing data: writing code from plain-language requests, documenting each step, cleaning and standardizing values, spotting anomalies, and matching records from different sources.

Why

Informatica says data teams spend up to 80% of their time preparing data instead of analyzing it. Agility at Scale, citing IBM, puts preparation at 50 to 70% of project time. The research notes that its sources disagree on the share.

Informatica says poor data quality costs enterprises USD 12.9 million a year on average. It names no study behind the figure.

ITTech Pulse advises treating any saving as a hypothesis to test against a baseline. A CIO quoted in CIO.com says the real test is whether tools improve the integrity of the data, not how fast they work.

How

CHI Software suggests starting with high-impact, low-risk, repeatable work such as documentation, and putting a governance layer in place before scaling: who can view or edit data, where it comes from and goes, and how changes and errors are tracked.

Kanerika describes AI proposing quality rules that a steward approves, and sending borderline record matches to a steward queue. Fivetran says anomalies should be flagged for review, not silently corrected.

DataHub says to record what the transformation code did at field level, at the time it ran.

§4.1

Cleaning and shaping the data

You are hereStandard
  • §4.1.1
    Five processing steps

    KNIME names five steps. Cleaning removes duplicates, corrects errors and fills missing values. Transformation converts raw or unstructured data into a usable structure. Integration combines separate sources. Reduction removes redundant or irrelevant data. Validation confirms the output meets standards and reflects its sources. §4.1.1

  • §4.1.2
    Processing activities

    HBS lists data wrangling (also called cleaning, munging or remediation), compression into a more storage-efficient format, encryption to address privacy concerns, and preparation: exploring, cleaning, enriching, transforming and organizing data for analytics, machine learning and AI. Digitizing a printed form also counts as processing. §4.1.2

  • §4.1.3
    Two further views

    Acceldata describes cleaning, transformation and integration in the same terms. Splunk treats processing as turning raw data into useful information through ordered steps, and describes it as a cyclic process. §4.1.3

  • §4.1.4
    Transformation in practice

    Redpanda describes transformation as normalizing values, filling gaps, converting types and extracting features, with an analysis-ready structure as the goal. Stream transformations include extracting a field such as a customer ID, normalizing dates, and anonymizing by removing personal data. §4.1.4

Who

Data engineers build the pipelines that extract, transform and load data. Data scientists explore the raw data to find useful sources and formats. §4.1.5a

Rules

Splunk says to monitor how data is actually used, to confirm it stays within standards and within legal and ethical limits. Its guide for this stage lists GDPR, CCPA, HIPAA, PCI DSS, PIPEDA, the UK Data Protection Act 2018 and the Australian Privacy Principles. §4.1.5b

Anonymization and removal of personal data are named types of stream transformation. §4.1.5b

Tools

Machine learning can automate cleaning, deduplication, anomaly detection and normalization, for structured and unstructured data. Agentic AI can monitor pipelines for duplicate spikes, schema changes and failed validation, then rerun steps or change approach. §4.1.5c

Named tools: ETL tools; Kafka Streams, Snowflake and Apache Spark; Apache Airflow and dbt; Hadoop, Python and JavaScript. §4.1.5c

What breaks

Duplicate spikes, schema changes and failed validation. Not meeting standards or regulations. Schema drift, an unexpected structural change that can break pipelines or corrupt analysis, for example after an API update. §4.1.5d

KNIME describes real-time quality metrics in its worked example. The master records no figure. §4.1.5d

Where AI can take the load

AI can clean and standardize at scale: fuzzy deduplication, normalizing formats and handling missing values, with learned baselines in place of fixed rules.

Why

Informatica and Kanerika say rule-based checks catch only known, predefined issues. Domo says AI can catch subtle drift, unexpected correlations between fields and gradual degradation.

How

AngelHack suggests layering AI anomaly detection over rule-based validation.

Teradata warns that cleaning that is too aggressive can remove signal, and advises lineage, audit logs and human review for critical fields.

§4.2

Batch processing

You are hereStandard
  • §4.2.1
    What batch processing is

    Data is buffered or queued, then processed when the buffer fills or an interval passes. Technologies named are Apache Hadoop, MapReduce, Spark, Storm and Flink. §4.2.1

  • §4.2.2
    Batch patterns

    MapReduce reads data blocks across nodes, shuffles the results and reduces them per node. A distributed join splits one logical join into smaller joins on each node. A broadcast join sends one small table to every node. A sort-merge join sorts both tables, then merges them instead of crossing every row. A shuffle hash join, used when neither table fits on one node, partitions both by join key and is more resource-intensive than a broadcast join. §4.2.2

Who

Not stated in the master’s sources. §4.2.3a

Rules

Not stated in the master’s sources. §4.2.3b

Tools

Apache Spark is a unified engine for batch and streaming. It is distributed, caches in memory, tolerates faults, reads and writes HDFS, Hive, Cassandra and Amazon S3, and supports Java, Scala, Python and R. §4.2.3c

What breaks

Redpanda lists best practices rather than failures: process out of order to reduce task dependencies, optimize memory (compression, cache optimization, memory pooling), and process data in place on the node where it is stored. §4.2.3d

§4.3

Real-time (stream) processing

You are hereStandard
  • §4.3.1
    What it is and why

    Data is ingested, analyzed and processed continuously as it is generated. Redpanda lists the benefits as operational efficiency, user experience and scalability. §4.3.1

  • §4.3.2
    Parts of an event-driven design

    Input sources, a stream processor, processing logic written in Java, Python or Scala, state management, event processors and windowing, a computational model, and output streams to stores such as HDFS, Cassandra or HBase. §4.3.2

  • §4.3.3
    Streaming patterns

    Windowing (grouping events by a key such as user ID, or by a time range), triggering, handling late arrivals (discard them or process them separately), stateful processing, real-time joins, aggregation and filtering, routing, and transforming by extracting, normalizing or anonymizing. §4.3.3

  • §4.3.4
    Types of window

    Keyed windows group by a key; non-keyed windows do not. Windows may be fixed or variable in size and are processed one at a time for parallelism. They may be time-based or count-based subsets. §4.3.4

  • §4.3.5
    Technologies

    Apache Storm, Flink, Spark Streaming and Kafka Streams; AWS Kinesis; Azure Stream Analytics. Spark Streaming splits a stream into mini-batches. Flink offers event-time processing, stateful computation, exactly-once guarantees and unified batch and stream processing. §4.3.5

  • §4.3.6
    Challenges for developers

    Fault tolerance, data consistency, privacy and security, latency, diverse serialization formats (JSON, Avro, Protobuf, binary), schema variability across sources, delayed or out-of-order data, exactly-once and at-least-once processing, and shifting business demands. §4.3.6

  • §4.3.7
    Best practices

    Minimize input and output, since disk is typically the bottleneck, using micro-batching and efficient serialization. Distribute, partition and shard data to balance load. Process in memory and cache for low latency. §4.3.7

Who

Not stated in the master’s sources. §4.3.8a

Rules

Strong security and access restrictions where direct access to data is limited, and protection of sensitive data. §4.3.8b

Tools

Checkpointing saves application state to durable storage; Flink persists state; watermarking handles time skew; monitoring and logging guide scaling out or up. §4.3.8c

What breaks

Out-of-order events, loss of state on failure, and consumer overload. The source also shows a "password redaction" example that replaces only the label and leaves the value visible; the master records it as a documentation defect, not a recommended practice. §4.3.8d

§4.4

Orchestration and transformation tools

You are hereStandard
  • §4.4.1
    Apache Airflow

    Workflow orchestration in Python, with workflows defined as directed graphs. Its parts are a web server, a scheduler, workers and a metadata database. It monitors and alerts on task status, and has operators for Snowflake and Tableau. §4.4.1

  • §4.4.2
    dbt

    A command-line tool for SQL-based transformations inside the warehouse. It supports ELT and is a transformation layer only: it neither extracts nor loads. §4.4.2

  • §4.4.3
    Flink and Kafka Streams

    Apache Flink and Kafka Streams handle real-time processing. The source gives five-minute windowed fraud detection as the Kafka Streams example. §4.4.3

  • §4.4.4
    The tool category

    Transformation tools cleanse, validate and transform data, and improve pipeline efficiency and quality. §4.4.4

  • §4.4.5
    Batch and stream together

    The Lambda architecture has a batch layer, a speed layer for real-time work such as anomaly detection, and a serving layer; its drawback is running two systems with synchronized code. One source says its serving layer typically uses a caching layer such as Apache Spark or a CDN; the master notes that Spark is a processing engine, so it treats that as a source inconsistency. The Kappa architecture, proposed by Jay Kreps, removes the batch layer and treats everything as a stream over an immutable log of events. §4.4.5

Who

Data engineers. §4.4.6a

Rules

Not stated in the master’s sources. §4.4.6b

Tools

Spark jobs are scheduled and monitored with Airflow, which alerts on failures or delays. §4.4.6c

What breaks

The complexity of running Lambda's two layers. Spark keeps processing if some nodes fail. §4.4.6d

Where AI can take the load

Orchestration can learn from past runs, and AI can detect schema drift, predict failures and trace their root cause.

Why

DataHub says preparation is the least observable stage: reading pipeline code later shows what it does today, not what it did when a given record passed through.

How

Domo advises defining service levels and baseline metrics, putting anomaly models on key pipelines, setting alert thresholds and escalation paths, and writing runbooks for common failures.

Neurealm describes orchestration AI that pauses a pipeline and alerts the owner with a suggested fix; the owner decides.

§4.5

Architecture patterns for data flow

You are hereStandard
  • §4.5.1
    Principles

    Redpanda lists loose coupling, scalability, reliability, security built in from the start, and flexibility. §4.5.1

  • §4.5.2
    Patterns

    A data warehouse pattern extracts, transforms and loads into central structured storage; ELT warehouses transform inside it. A data lake pattern stores data as it is and transforms on demand, which is flexible but inefficient and expensive without management. A dataflow pipeline moves small messages through streams or topics. An IoT pipeline adds a gateway that filters, routes and aggregates data from limited devices; its failure modes are unstable connectivity and weak devices. §4.5.2

  • §4.5.3
    Newer architectures

    Data mesh, data fabric and metadata-first architecture are noted. §4.5.3

  • §4.5.4
    What shapes the choice

    Source attributes (how long data is kept after it is generated, push or pull capture, triggering events, duplicates), ingestion and storage characteristics, and the consumers: machine learning often needs large batches and business intelligence often needs real time. §4.5.4

Who

Not stated in the master’s sources. §4.5.5a

Rules

Security architecture from day one. §4.5.5b

Tools

A blueprint that does not depend on a technology, performance tracking for each component, and controlled change that leaves neighbouring interfaces unaffected. §4.5.5c

What breaks

Fallback mechanisms for lost connectivity or a failed component, aiming for little or no data loss. §4.5.5d

§4.6

Governed processing and usage

You are hereStandard
  • §4.6.1
    Activities

    Alation lists extract-transform-load, cleansing, normalization, aggregation and integration across systems. §4.6.1

  • §4.6.2
    AI uses in processing

    Alation names machine learning for pattern and anomaly detection, language processing for sentiment, and computer vision for product quality control. §4.6.2

  • §4.6.3
    Governing the work

    Alation lists version control for scripts, documented transformation logic, quality monitoring and audit trails. §4.6.3

  • §4.6.4
    Governed pipelines

    OvalEdge describes governed ETL or ELT pipelines that make transformations auditable: quality rules and standard definitions are applied during processing, not after; end-to-end lineage lets every metric be traced to its source; datasets are certified and given an owner before wide release. Undocumented logic spreads errors. §4.6.4

  • §4.6.5
    Usage and enrichment

    Atlan says ETL or ELT pipelines, cleaning, transformation and enrichment feed analytics tools, dashboards, AI agents and business applications. §4.6.5

  • §4.6.6
    An example

    In OvalEdge's example, nightly pipelines standardize currency, remove duplicate customers, validate products and certify datasets for sales reporting and forecasting. §4.6.6

  • §4.6.7
    Two views of processing

    The engineering sources treat processing as engineering. The governance sources add the controls that wrap it: version control, documented logic, certification and lineage. §4.6.7

Who

Ownership is assigned before release. Data scientists and data engineers act as in §4.1. §4.6.8a

Rules

Quality rules and standard definitions are applied in flight. Audit trails are kept. §4.6.8b

Tools

Governed pipelines and certification workflows. Atlan describes column-level lineage so that archiving or deleting one asset does not break another; the master marks this a vendor capability. §4.6.8c

Undocumented logic spreads errors. Dashboards and AI models depend on consistent processing. §4.6.8d

Where AI can take the load

AI can find and redact personal data before generative AI uses it. AWS describes Amazon Comprehend doing this on objects from a raw zone.

Why

AWS says redaction can remove the semantic context that a model's accuracy depends on.

04

Storage

§5.0OverviewStandardExpert
You are here

Storage keeps data accessible, protected and backed up: processed data held for future use, usually in databases or datasets, in places that are scalable and reliable. §5.0

In the journey · Stage 4Watch this stage

Where data is kept.

Storage keeps data accessible, protected and backed up. Tamsworth stores the clean Silver row beside Bronze, its raw copy, locks it and backs it up, then moves it to cheaper places as it ages.

What

Keep the row accessible and protected

The store must keep data accessible, protected and backed up. Database administrators manage the storage systems, with IT and security. Tamsworth keeps its raw Bronze copy and its clean Silver row side by side, with a place left for Gold.

Tools: Storage platforms: a data warehouse such as Snowflake, a data lake such as Amazon S3, or a lakehouse table format such as Delta Lake.

Owner: Database administrators, IT, Security

How

Land, organize, protect, back up

Tamsworth writes the row into the store, indexes it and splits it by date so it can be found fast, encrypts its five sensitive fields, locks it to the right people, and copies it to a second place. Protection matches how sensitive the data is, and a backup keeps a usable copy if the original is damaged.

Tools: Indexing and partitioning in the database; encryption at rest and role-based access control; backup to a second location.

Owner: Database administrators, IT, Security

Why

Not all data needs the fastest shelf

Newer, often-used data sits on faster, dearer storage; older data moves to cheaper storage. The master states the saving in words only. Tamsworth's example prices make it concrete: the tiered store comes out 78.4% cheaper than keeping everything warm and 93.8% cheaper than keeping everything hot.

Tools: Storage tiers in a cloud warehouse or lake, with lifecycle policies that move data between them.

Owner: Database administrators, IT

When

A retention rule sets the timing

Tamsworth's rule moves the row to warm after 30 days, to cold after 180 days, and archives it after 7 years. Storage cost is one of three things that shape such a rule, with compliance and business needs. Data owners define retention periods, and IT carries them out.

Tools: Retention and lifecycle policies in the warehouse or lake.

Owner: IT

Next

Management

Stage 5 keeps stored data accurate, compliant and secure: who may see it, what it means, and when it is archived or deleted.

Tools: Governance, access control and catalog tools.

Owner: Data stewards, Security, Compliance

With AIAct 2 · from the AI research file, not the master

Where AI can take the load

AI can take over some of the upkeep of a store: moving data between tiers by how it is used, forecasting capacity, tuning indexes and partitions, and watching access for unusual activity.

Why

AvePoint says some of its customers saved up to 60% on storage through automated archiving and version control. IDC, in a study DataHub commissioned, reports customers saving USD 250,000 to 300,000 a year by finding redundant and unused data assets. The research found no independently measured saving.

AvePoint says the storage bill is the symptom and unmanaged sprawl is the cause. DataHub says storage matters least on its own, because stored data that cannot be found, understood or trusted is unusable.

How

Agility at Scale says to match each tier to the data's current usage, and to measure savings against what storage would have cost without lifecycle-driven migration.

AvePoint describes a person simulating the affected items and the projected savings before anything runs, and owners attesting to a workspace's purpose before it is retired. TierPoint and Rivery frame storage AI as recommending actions within guardrails, and neither names who approves.

AI also changes what storage holds. DataHub says new stores appear, such as feature stores and vector databases, with the same data in several shapes. AvePoint says copilots and agents can reach any content they can find, so stale or misclassified stored data becomes a security and accuracy risk.

§5.1

Storage architectures

You are hereStandard
  • §5.1.1
    Databases

    Relational databases such as MySQL, PostgreSQL and MariaDB hold structured data in tables and rows, with the schema set before writing. NoSQL databases hold unstructured and semi-structured data, with the schema set when the data is read: key-value, column, document and graph stores. §5.1.1

  • §5.1.2
    Data warehouse

    A warehouse holds structured, curated data under a set schema, usually loaded in batches by ETL with business rules. Snowflake, Amazon Redshift, Google BigQuery and Vertica are named. Updates are hard and need stakeholders, batch process changes and testing. §5.1.2

  • §5.1.3
    Data lake

    A lake holds raw and processed data in any format, with no schema imposed until it is read, usually loaded by ELT. Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage and Azure Data Lake Storage are named for the cloud. A lake without metadata management turns into a "data swamp", an unorganized pile of sources. §5.1.3

  • §5.1.4
    Data hub

    A hub is a central point that mediates between sources and users, with layers and zones that separate data by quality, purpose and access. It stores no data directly, though it may act as a store for its consumers. §5.1.4

  • §5.1.5
    Data lakehouse

    A lakehouse puts warehouse-style management on low-cost, open lake storage: transactions, table versions and quality checks. Delta Lake, Apache Hudi and Apache Iceberg are named. One source describes it in words that read like a lake definition, and the master treats the warehouse-versus-lake page as the stronger definition. §5.1.5

  • §5.1.6
    Warehouse against lake

    The two differ in schema (on write or on read), format, timeliness, processing and users. Warehouses serve analysts and stakeholders with regular dashboards; lakes serve data scientists and engineers with varied, heavy workloads such as model training. A Gartner survey of June 2020 is cited for how many executives had invested in each. §5.1.6

  • §5.1.7
    Recommendations

    One source calls a lakehouse the most performant and cost-effective option, and advises keeping warehouse concepts for schema design and ETL logic. §5.1.7

  • §5.1.8
    What the sources do not cover

    The warehouse-versus-lake page does not cover governance, security, medallion (bronze, silver, gold) layers, tiering, detailed cost models or roles beyond user types. The journey's Bronze, Silver and Gold are Tamsworth's own architecture, not a general layer model from the master. §5.1.8

Who

Database administrators manage storage systems; IT staff and security teams ensure security and backup. Warehouse users are BI analysts and stakeholders; lake users are data analysts, engineers and scientists. Centralized management gives better governance but harder scaling; distributed management gives teams autonomy at the risk of inconsistency. §5.1.9a

Rules

Splunk lists the storage protocols to set: backups, archiving, retention policies, database maintenance, encryption and user authentication. Varonis says to protect data according to its sensitivity or importance, and to have policies for environments that hold inactive data. §5.1.9b

Tools

Data lakes and warehouses on cloud platforms. AI can analyze access patterns to recommend indexing, partitioning or tiered storage, and agentic AI can monitor usage, access and compliance rules and trigger approved retention changes, backups or access-control recommendations. Predictive storage forecasts growth to avoid overprovisioning. §5.1.9c

What breaks

Security gaps and backup failures. Corruption or compromise of the original source, reduced by redundancy. On-premises hardware that lacks scalability and carries a greater risk of data loss. The data swamp. §5.1.9d

You are hereStandard

Redpanda adds version control and backups of data, transformation logic, configurations and schemas. Splunk calls for regular backups and disaster recovery plans, and Acceldata for one backup copy kept in immutable storage. §5.3.1

IT staff and security teams. §5.3.3a

Rules

Protocols for backups and archiving (Splunk), and for backup, disaster recovery and incident response. §5.3.3b

Where AI can take the load

AI can watch stored data for unusual access or large transfers that may signal a breach. As an example, two vendors cite Google's Big Sleep project of 2025, in which an AI agent found an exploit before attackers used it and engineers patched it.

Why

IBM, in a report it promotes, puts the global average cost of a data breach at USD 4.99 million, with AI-driven attacks up 56%.

How

Kanerika says an AI feature needs the same controls as any privileged user: limit what it can read, mask sensitive fields in non-production copies and log every access.

AWS says to encrypt embeddings at rest and to apply role-based access control to vector stores. It says embeddings "typically contain private and sensitive data", so a vector store becomes a new store of sensitive data.

§5.4

Tiering and ageing

You are hereStandard
  • §5.4.1
    The general principle

    Newer or often-used data sits on faster, dearer media; older data moves to cheaper storage. A lifecycle tool sorts data into tiers by policy and migrates it as its value and relevance change. Hierarchical storage management (HSM) automates the choice of media by cost and performance, and the master records it as "simply one tool", not the whole of lifecycle management. §5.4.1

  • §5.4.2
    The Splunk bucket lifecycle

    In Splunk's example, data lands hot (up to 24 hours), is warm for 30 days, cold for 30 days, then frozen: archived or deleted. Size and age can both trigger a move, and when a size cap is reached the least recently used warm buckets roll on. Volumes can separate hot, warm and cold data. These periods are Splunk's examples. Splunk Cloud's dynamic tiers appear only in search results and are not used here. §5.4.2

  • §5.4.3
    Streaming storage tiers

    Redpanda keeps frequently used data in a fast tier and moves less-used data to a cheaper one, by default cloud object storage. Kafka retention policies and log segment management can cause high disk use and cost. §5.4.3

Who

IT teams implement and maintain the platform (Splunk). §5.4.4a

Rules

Storage constraints and cost are one of three inputs to a retention policy, with compliance and business needs. §5.4.4b

Tools

Splunk's index settings for the bucket lifecycle; storage threshold alerts and a ballast file in Redpanda. §5.4.4c

What breaks

Too aggressive a reduction of Splunk's index files hurts search performance. If no archive directory is set, frozen data is deleted by default. Log growth that nobody manages in Kafka. §5.4.4d

With AIAct 2 · from the AI research file, not the master

Where AI can take the load

AI can set tiering rules from usage patterns: busy data on fast storage, rarely used data on cheaper storage. OvalEdge, TierPoint and others describe this; TierPoint says where data lives and how it moves is no longer a static practice. Rivery says AI can predict when data will be needed and suggest when to archive, replicate or compress it.

Why

OvalEdge, Rivery and Kreate Technologies say tiering reduces storage cost while keeping critical data accessible. None gives a figure.

How

AvePoint says to simulate which items would be affected, and the projected savings, before anything runs, and lets the user pick a conservative or aggressive setting. Agility at Scale says to measure savings against a baseline without lifecycle-driven migration.

Storage for streaming and scale

You are hereStandard

    Log-based storage

    Kafka appends to immutable commit logs partitioned across brokers. Redpanda uses an approach that merges smaller segments into larger ones, with data-skipping to reach the segments it needs. §5.5.1

  • §5.5.2
    Compression

    Spark Streaming, Flink, Kafka and Redpanda each offer compression, with codecs such as Snappy, LZ4, ZSTD and gzip. The source page's CPU comparison is an illustrative example and cannot be verified independently. §5.5.2

  • §5.5.3
    Scaling

    Horizontal scaling adds machines; vertical scaling strengthens nodes; the two can be combined. §5.5.3

Who

Not stated in the master’s sources. §5.5.4a

Rules

Not stated in the master’s sources. §5.5.4b

Tools

Tiered storage, and Redpanda's self-healing. §5.5.4c

What breaks

Disk growth, log compaction needs, and throughput and latency under load. §5.5.4d

§5.6

Security, resilience and tiering rules

You are hereStandard
  • §5.6.1
    Storage choice

    Structured data typically goes to relational databases and unstructured data to NoSQL or non-relational databases. Assess the infrastructure for vulnerabilities, then apply protections such as encryption. The location can be cloud, on premises or hybrid; the choice balances performance, cost, access frequency and compliance. §5.6.1

  • §5.6.2
    Security

    Encryption at rest and in transit, role-based access control and network segmentation. OvalEdge says encryption at rest for health and payment data should come with periodic key rotation. §5.6.2

  • §5.6.3
    Resilience

    Backup strategies with several recovery points, automated testing, and recovery time and recovery point objectives (RTO and RPO). Stored copies act as backups against deletion, corruption, accidental change and attacks such as malware. Rimage says to define a backup process for redundancy and keep a log of storage locations and data movements. §5.6.3

  • §5.6.4
    Tiering rules

    Tiered storage runs hot, warm, cold, archive. Consolidating storage reduces silos and eases lineage tracking. Cloud storage classes range from immediate retrieval to long-term archive. OvalEdge gives an example, marked illustrative: recent transactions in a high-speed warehouse, and data older than 90 days moved to encrypted object storage with 7-year retention. §5.6.4

  • §5.6.5
    Storage architecture documentation

    Document tiers, retention periods, migration policies, backup frequency and disaster recovery; monitoring, capacity planning, automated alerts and escalation; and the configurations, access controls and audit trails that show compliance. §5.6.5

  • §5.6.6
    Regulations tied to storage

    Alation names the HIPAA technical safeguards and GDPR for European residents' personal data. Rimage names HIPAA, SOX, GDPR and CCPA. IBM cites GDPR as a way to avoid costly fines. None is tied to a retention period. §5.6.6

Who

Stated in part. IBM and Rimage name no role. Alation assigns storage planning to the owners of the data management plan. §5.6.7a

Rules

Stated in part. Rimage says GDPR fines can reach "$20 million Euro or 4% of your annual revenue", in its own wording. The master gives no other policy for this pillar. §5.6.7b

Tools

Automated alerts and escalation. Automated retention rules by data type, department or regulation: OvalEdge's example, marked illustrative, is five years for financial records. §5.6.7c

What breaks

Poor design raises infrastructure cost and security exposure. Without retention rules, audits and legal responses slow down. RTO and RPO are the named resilience measures. §5.6.7d

Where AI can take the load

AI-driven security tools can analyze patterns and anomalies and start protective measures such as encryption or access limits. Rivery and TierPoint describe this; Boldare says AI is often used to change encryption methods live.

Why

Aligning storage with lifecycle requirements, rather than deciding the architecture in isolation, is Agility at Scale's advice.

How

AngelHack lists encryption at rest and in transit and fine-grained access control that can restrict fields or rows. Kiteworks says to check where a tool runs against data-residency duties, and ITTech Pulse advises asking the same of any AI service.

§5.7

Organizing, efficiency and infrastructure

You are hereStandard
  • §5.7.1
    Organization of stored data

    Locations include physical servers, cloud storage and digital file repositories. Compyl says to develop a naming protocol and a document workflow. A centralized structure prevents silos, and knowing where each user's data sits supports GDPR records requests. Sensitive data can be stored automatically in a secure environment. §5.7.1

  • §5.7.2
    Storage options and their fit

    Warehouses fit structured data, lakes fit raw data in its native format, and cloud object storage fits semi-structured and unstructured data with tiered access. Structured data typically uses relational databases; unstructured data may use object storage or NoSQL. §5.7.2

  • §5.7.3
    Efficiency techniques

    Deduplication removes duplicate files or blocks, and compression reduces stored size. Together they shrink the footprint, cut cost and speed up backups. §5.7.3

  • §5.7.4
    Backup and archive strategies

    Backups are short-term copies for quick recovery. Archives are long-term storage for data that is rarely used but valuable. Incremental or differential backups are preferred to full ones: an incremental backup captures only what changed since the last backup. §5.7.4

  • §5.7.5
    Storage tiering

    Frequently used data stays on high-performance systems, and older data moves to cheaper cold or object storage, which lowers cost while keeping data available. Automated tiering moves data and backups between tiers as they age. §5.7.5

  • §5.7.6
    Safeguards for stored data

    Encryption, transformation and redundancy against breaches, corruption and accidental loss. §5.7.6

  • §5.7.7
    Availability infrastructure

    Scalable cloud storage centralizes data and reduces fragmentation. Redundancy and backups copy data across servers or clouds so another system can take over on failure. Load balancing spreads traffic. Disaster recovery covers natural disasters, cyberattacks and system failures, with restoration protocols that limit downtime and data loss. Box adds that backups can be kept in secure vaults. §5.7.7

  • §5.7.8
    Hybrid multicloud and recovery guidance

    In Nutanix's answers, unified visibility across public and private clouds, automated tiering and standard security controls improve lifecycle management. Lifecycle policies keep backups and replicas consistent and current, shorten recovery, and restore only the relevant data on failover. Without lifecycle management, backup environments become bloated and costly. §5.7.8

  • §5.7.9
    Protection practices at rest

    Encryption at rest and in transit, access logging with anomaly detection, and quarterly penetration testing. §5.7.9

Who

Stated in part. IT teams and outside IT help are named only for integration challenges. Three of the sources name no storage role. §5.7.10a

Rules

Retention policies that name GDPR, HIPAA and PCI DSS (Nutanix), and GDPR records requests (Compyl). None is tied to a retention period. §5.7.10b

Tools

Cloud lifecycle policies and data management software: AWS Lifecycle Manager, Microsoft Azure Storage Lifecycle and Nutanix Data Lens. Nutanix Objects is described, by the vendor, as scalable immutable storage for long-term retention. §5.7.10c

What breaks

Data sprawl, bloated backup environments, silos and legacy systems. Nutanix cites Statista for the figure that users retain only 2% of data year over year; the master records no other figure. §5.7.10d

Smart tiering and lifecycle automation can move data and backups by usage and policy. Informatica describes lifecycle management, automated retention, storage optimization and cost governance as one vendor "pillar".

Why

Pentaho says the habit of storing everything has become a budgetary crisis and a strategic risk, and that redundant and trivial content inflates storage bills while degrading signals for AI. It names no figure. The research notes sources disagree on how much storage matters on its own.

05

Management

§6.0OverviewStandardExpert
You are here

Management keeps data accurate, complete and secure across its whole life. It runs alongside every other stage, not after one. KNIME lists its parts as governance, quality, security, access and retrieval, integration, and archiving and deletion. §6.0, §1.3

In the journey · Stage 5Watch this stage

Part 1 of 2Who may see data, and what it means.

Management runs alongside every stage and keeps data accurate, complete and secure. At Tamsworth Health, the stored Silver row gets a description, rules on who may read it, and a record of every read.

What

Governance runs alongside every stage

Management keeps data accurate, complete and secure through its whole life, so it runs beside every stage, not after Storage. Data stewards, security and compliance teams set its policies and standards. Tamsworth marks five fields of the Silver row as sensitive, because together they identify a patient.

Tools: Governance platforms, data catalogs and master data management.

Owner: Data stewards, Security, Compliance

How

Describe, restrict, record

A catalog holds the metadata that says where each field came from, what form it takes and what it means. Access control gives each role only what it needs, and masks sensitive fields where full access is not needed. An audit log records who read the data, when and how.

Tools: Data catalogs, such as Microsoft Purview Data Catalog, IBM Watson Knowledge Catalog or Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Data Catalog; role-based access control with masking; audit logs.

Owner: Data stewards, Security

Why

So people can trust what they read

Low-quality data skews analysis and leads to poor decisions. The trace, which the master calls lineage, shows where data came from; it matters for quality and is required for compliance in regulated sectors. Tamsworth's trace runs from the Silver row back through the clean copy and the raw copy to the bedside monitor.

Tools: Lineage tools, such as Apache Atlas.

Owner: Data stewards

When

At every request

Each time someone asks to read the row, the rules are checked, the answer is shaped to their role, and the read is logged. At Tamsworth a clinician sees the full row, an analyst sees it with the five sensitive fields hidden, and an outside party is turned away. Quality is checked all the time too, not once.

Tools: Role-based or attribute-based access control; data quality checks, such as Great Expectations.

Owner: Security, Data stewards

Next

Part 2: how long it lives

Next come the rules about time: how long Tamsworth keeps the row, when it is archived, and when it must be deleted.

Owner: Compliance, IT

With AIAct 2 · from the AI research file, not the master

Where AI can take the load

AI can do much of the routine work of describing data: drafting metadata and descriptions, spotting sensitive fields by what they hold rather than what they are called, and mapping where data flows from query logs.

Why

Agility at Scale calls classification the foundation of every other lifecycle decision: without it, retention cannot be enforced and tiering is guesswork. Concentric AI says manual classification leaves too much room for error and does not scale.

The research found no independently measured benefit. The only figures come from one implementer's case and one vendor's case.

How

OvalEdge says to build the catalog first. Without it, AI tools cannot reason about the data they are asked to manage.

DataHub gives a test of a working program. For any table, on any day, someone can say who owns it, what feeds it, what breaks if it changes, which models and agents have read it, and whether anything would notice if it went away.

Knowing the data
§6.5

Metadata, catalog and lineage

You are hereStandard
  • §6.5.1
    Metadata management

    Metadata records where data came from, what form it takes and what it means. Splunk says to manage it by a standard process, name who keeps it up to date, and review it regularly. §6.5.1

  • §6.5.2
    Catalogs and indexes

    A catalog gathers metadata in one place, so data can be found, understood, checked and shown to be compliant. Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Data Catalog, IBM Watson Knowledge Catalog and Microsoft Purview Data Catalog are named. Splunk notes that such tools are resource-hungry, need expertise and often cost a lot. §6.5.2

  • §6.5.3
    Lineage

    Lineage tracks where data came from, which matters for quality and reliability. Warehouses keep it through their scripts; lakes need metadata management. Apache Atlas is named for tracing data origin, which regulated sectors need for compliance. What lineage each stage must record is not stated. §6.5.3

  • §6.5.4
    Documentation

    Redpanda treats continuous documentation as a required step of a pipeline, in tools such as Confluence and GitHub Wiki. §6.5.4

  • §6.5.5
    Splunk's metadata practices

    Splunk lists source types, target indexes, searches for sensitive data, field extractions, tags, a corporate information model and naming conventions. §6.5.5

Who

The roles that keep metadata up to date must be defined (Splunk). KNIME has data stewards keep the records. §6.5.6a

Rules

Lineage is required for compliance in regulated sectors. §6.5.6b

Tools

AI-assisted metadata enrichment and classification; search and sorting of data by meaning, using language processing. §6.5.6c

What breaks

Without metadata, a lake becomes a data swamp. Transformations nobody documented cost trust across teams. §6.5.6d

Why

Domo lists the least metadata every asset needs before it is usable: a name and description, an owner and steward, a sensitivity class, lineage back to its sources, and quality measures. It warns that wrong lineage mapping breaks the audit trail downstream.

You are hereStandard

Data stewards; certification in the catalog authorizes use cases (Alation). §6.11.5a

Catalog tools (see the tooling pillar) and automated metadata discovery. §6.11.5c

Not stated in the master’s sources. §6.6.5d

§6.8

Redundant, obsolete and trivial data

You are hereStandard
  • §6.8.1
    What counts

    Duplicates, files untouched for years, data past its retention window, and unused backups, archives, media and logs. Varonis says its product finds this data and quarantines it automatically. §6.8.1

  • §6.8.2
    Finding it

    Varonis judges staleness from a record's age and time since last access, combined with its classification and permissions, and finds stale data hidden inside active folders. §6.8.2

  • §6.8.3
    Duplicates

    Copies are grouped, with the original and newest marked, and shown with where each lives and whether it is sensitive, overexposed or past retention. The data owner chooses which copy to keep. §6.8.3

  • §6.8.4
    The value claimed

    Varonis claims lower storage cost, cleaner data for AI, fewer audit findings and less damage if breached. It gives no figures. §6.8.4

  • §6.8.5
    Shadow data

    The term does not appear in the first batch of sources. The nearest named risks there are forgotten sensitive data, duplicates and stale data. §6.8.5

Who

The data owners choose which duplicate to keep; "owner" is a filter in the tool. §6.8.6a

Rules

Built-in, editable policies for duplicates, stale data and retention. §6.8.6b

Tools

Automatic quarantine, built on the classification, permissions and activity data of Varonis's platform. §6.8.6c

What breaks

Paying to store data nobody uses, and AI answering from stale data. The source gives no savings figures. §6.8.6d

§6.12

Lifecycle policy as code

You are hereStandard
  • §6.12.1
    Policies that move data

    Atlan names five kinds: storage tiering (retention, archival, disposal, destruction), freshness, usage, quality and integrity, and access control as sensitivity changes. §6.12.1

  • §6.12.2
    Policy as code

    A rule is defined once and applies automatically to every asset it covers, updating everywhere when it changes. §6.12.2

  • §6.12.3
    Tags that trigger actions

    Governance tags can start lifecycle actions: a dataset whose certification is withdrawn can be archived automatically. Actions can also fire when sensitive data is reclassified. §6.12.3

  • §6.12.4
    What automation keys on

    Classification, sensitivity, ownership, regulation or last access. OvalEdge's example pilot archives customer data untouched for 12 months. §6.12.4

  • §6.12.5

    Atlan says moving data between stages "is the core goal, and automation enables it"; IBM says data moves on as tasks are completed or requirements are met. §6.12.5

Who

Ownership may vary across teams, which is acceptable if processes are automated and documented consistently. §6.12.6a

Rules

Map each policy to the team that owns it, so it can be applied in practice. §6.12.6b

Tools

Cloud lifecycle features and governance platforms; freshness and quality checks feeding the policies. §6.12.6c

If metadata cannot drive enforcement automatically, lifecycle management fails. §6.12.6d

Compliance, measures, what goes wrong
§6.7

Compliance, audit and regulations

You are hereStandard
  • §6.7.1
    Regulations named

    GDPR, HIPAA, CCPA and PCI DSS across the first sources; PIPEDA, the UK Data Protection Act 2018 and the Australian Privacy Principles in one. GDPR's right to be forgotten lets a person ask for their data to be erased. None is tied to a retention period. §6.7.1

  • §6.7.2
    Compliance measures

    Audit and monitor how data is used, assess security regularly, scan data, train people, and use an automated governance platform. The barriers named are thin resources, weak understanding of the rules and weak security. §6.7.2

  • §6.7.3
    Audit trails

    Access logs and change logs record who reached data and what they changed. Splunk documents every retention change with its reason, the people involved and the date. §6.7.3

  • §6.7.5
    More regulations, from the second batch

    SOX, Basel III and NIST SP 800-88 for regulated data at deletion. Data subject requests must be met across production, archive and backup. Some rules require long-term archive and forbid deletion; others require destruction and forbid keeping any copy. §6.7.5

  • §6.7.6
    More regulations, from the third batch

    GDPR, HIPAA, CCPA, PCI DSS and CMMC. GDPR and CCPA require deletion on request. Frameworks often require privacy and security policies with set destruction processes and timeframes. §6.7.6

Who

Legal and compliance units set the shortest and longest retention periods (Splunk). §6.7.4a

Rules

Documentation, audits and privacy policies; audits of retention. §6.7.4b

Tools

Varonis policies for lifecycle, retention and residency by department, server, data type and sensitivity; quarantine when GDPR data is exposed. §6.7.4c

What breaks

Regulatory fines, damage to reputation and audit findings. §6.7.4d

Challenges, risks and failure modes

You are hereStandard

    Silos and scale, missing quality measures, no accountability or auditing, and too little infrastructure to enforce policy. §6.17.1

    Fragmented, unclassified, untracked data, such as old spreadsheets and forgotten cloud files, with financial, operational and legal costs. §6.17.4

    Lifecycle policies prepare a business for breaches, data loss and system failure. IBM's promotional block puts the average breach at USD 4.99 million. §6.17.5

    Alation cites a projection of 463 exabytes of data created each day by 2025. §6.17.6

As listed above. §6.17.13d

§6.1

Governance framework

    Documents that set expectations, responsibilities, procedures and goals, and the rules for protecting, checking and sharing data. The three goals named are confidentiality, integrity and availability. §6.1.1

Data stewards, security, compliance and database governance teams set policies and standards (KNIME). Splunk has data owners define retention periods, IT carry them out and legal ensure compliance. §6.1.6a

See the roles pillar. §6.10.7a

AI inside the lifecycle

    Varonis names four: stale files surface in AI answers as if current; duplicates give conflicting answers; forgotten sensitive data is exposed once an assistant is connected; and deletion does not reach an AI pipeline's cache, index or derived data. §6.9.1

With AIAct 2 · from the AI research file, not the master

Where AI can take the load

AvePoint warns that AI may surface content that should have been archived or disposed of years ago.

Why

Epiq says extra data makes it harder for people and AI to find the right answer, and that cutting data down, defensibly, reduces the mistakes generative AI makes.

How

Kanerika gives a readiness check before any AI reads your data: every source has a named owner and a "last reviewed" date, documents carry classifications, and access follows the user, so an assistant never shows someone data they could not open themselves.

Kanerika's warning example: an outdated policy document in an AI's source library gets quoted with full confidence. DataHub adds that the same data can sit as a warehouse record, a feature-store row and a vector chunk, and a model of the lifecycle built on locations cannot see they are the same.

Getting ready for AI agents

  • §6.19.1

    Atlan says lifecycle policy should sit where agents read, not in a separate document, because agents take data as they find it and cannot tell current data from data that should have been archived. §6.19.1

  • §6.19.2
