    Lifecycle management keeps data fresh, traced and deleted on time, so agents work from current, reliable data. Atlan reports a 38% gain in query accuracy from governed context, its own claim. §6.19.2

  • §6.19.3

    IBM presents AI data management, with AI classification, natural-language queries and anomaly detection, as an answer to shadow data, poor quality and security risk. §6.19.3

    Alation says strong lifecycle practices, built on governance, automation and accountability, are what prepare an organization for AI. §6.19.4

Who

Not stated in the master’s sources. §6.19.5a

Rules

Not stated in the master’s sources. §6.19.5b

Tools

Vendor features from Atlan for giving agents governed context; AI classification (IBM). §6.19.5c

What breaks

Agents working from stale data. §6.19.5d

With AIAct 2 · from the AI research file, not the master

Where AI can take the load

DataHub says data now serves dashboards, model training, AI assistants and agents, and claims its product gives people and agents the same context.

Why

In DataHub's own survey, 82% of data and IT leaders said they would trust AI agents with high-stakes tasks even without reliable context, lineage and governance in place. DataHub reads this as trust running ahead of the foundations.

How

DataHub points out that the user is no longer always a person. A dashboard user can ask a colleague or notice a wrong chart; an agent does neither. Without context it can read, it does not pause, it answers anyway.

Controls on AI use

You are hereStandard

    Why AI raises the stakes

    BigID notes that ordinary applications fetch only the records asked for, while AI systems search, combine, summarize and act on much wider data, across assistants, search, training, vector databases and agents. §6.24.1

  • §6.24.2

    Stale data gives stale answers; duplicates split trust; sensitive data gains new audiences when a rarely used dataset is connected to an assistant; and deletion must reach AI systems. §6.24.2

↳

Retention and archival

§10.0OverviewStandardExpert
You are hereTold in Stage 5, part 2

Retention keeps data for a set time to meet legal, administrative, operational and business needs. Archival keeps data that is no longer in daily use but is still needed, safe and apart. Some models, Redpanda among them, count this as a stage of its own; KNIME puts archiving inside management, and so does this journey. §10.0, §1.3, §1.2.7c

In the journey · Stage 5Watch this stage

Part 2 of 2How long data lives.

Management also decides how long data is kept, and when it goes. Tamsworth keeps the Silver row for 7 years, then archives it. It is deleted when its keep-period ends, or when a person asks to be erased.

What

Decide how long data lives

Retention keeps data for a set time to meet legal, operational and business needs. Archival keeps data that is no longer in daily use but is still needed, apart from active data and ready to restore. Deletion removes it for good. Some models count retention and deletion as stages of their own; KNIME puts them inside management, and so does this journey.

Tools: Retention policies and archive stores, such as Google Vault or Bloomberg Vault.

Owner: Compliance, IT

How

Keep, archive, then delete on the rule

Data owners set how long each kind of data is kept, IT carries it out, and legal makes sure the rules are met. The period depends on regulation, business need, storage cost and how sensitive the data is. Tamsworth keeps the row in the store for 7 years, then archives it, and deletes it when its keep-period ends.

Tools: Retention and lifecycle policies that archive and delete on schedule.

Owner: IT, Compliance

Why

Keeping too long is a risk too

Data kept past its use still carries risk: more exposure in a breach, more to search in a lawsuit, more for AI to pick up. A retention policy without reliable deletion becomes an over-retention policy. Deleting what the law says to keep is also a failure, so every deletion is checked first.

Owner: Compliance, Security

When

When the period ends, or a person asks

Deletion is due when the keep-period ends, or when a person asks to be erased. Tamsworth first checks that no legal hold applies, then moves the data to quarantine, where it can still be undone. Every copy is then found, removed and checked, including copies held for AI, and the deletion is logged with its reason, policy, approver and proof.

Tools: Privacy and compliance tools that run deletion workflows, such as BigID or Securiti.

Owner: Security, Compliance, Data stewards

Next

Analysis

The governed rows go on to analysis, where four questions are asked of them: what happened, why, what may happen, and what to do.

Owner: Analysts, Data scientists, Business stakeholders

With AIAct 2 · from the AI research file, not the master

Where AI can take the load

CHI Software describes generative AI reading usage, compliance needs and long-term value to suggest which files are still useful and which should move to cold storage.

Why

AvePoint says every terabyte kept past its retention period is unmonitored sensitive data inside the reach of a breach, an insider or a legal discovery request. Pentaho calls for a shift from "keep everything" to "keep what creates value".

The research found no measured benefit specific to retention.

How

The sources disagree on how far AI may go. Kanerika says AI recommends and never automates: a person always approves, with an audit trail. OvalEdge says AI can trigger archiving when data becomes obsolete. The master holds both views and does not settle them.

§10.1

Designing a retention policy

You are hereStandard
  • §10.1.1
    What shapes a policy

    Regulation, with industry and regional minimums and maximums (GDPR, HIPAA and PCI DSS are named); business need; storage cost; and how often data is used, how sensitive it is, and the risk of keeping it longer. §10.1.1

  • §10.1.2
    Kinds of data

    Critical data, such as personal and financial records, is kept longest; operational logs for troubleshooting, shorter; analytical data, as the business needs; temporary data such as caches, hours or days. §10.1.2

  • §10.1.3
    Retention by classification

    Varonis maps retention windows to classification. Its examples: payment card data 7 years, personal data 2, health data 6. They are examples, not rules. §10.1.3

  • §10.1.4
    Examples elsewhere

    HBS and Redpanda's lifecycle page give no periods; Redpanda's streaming default is 24 hours. §10.1.4

  • §10.1.5
    Writing it down

    Define categories, set a period for each, describe deletion and archival, note exceptions, review when operations, rules or systems change, and record the reasons. §10.1.5

Who

Data owners define retention periods, IT carries them out, and legal makes sure regulations are met; legal and compliance set the shortest and longest periods; business units have differing needs (Splunk). §10.1.6a

Rules

Periods vary by regulation. Too short risks penalties; too long raises storage cost and breach exposure. §10.1.6b

Tools

See the Splunk example and policy-driven automation pillars. §10.1.6c

What breaks

The one usage measure stated is search counts by index. §10.1.6d

With AIAct 2 · from the AI research file, not the master

Where AI can take the load

AvePoint says its product can recommend retention rules by industry and region, citing the legislation. That is the vendor's claim.

Why

Kanerika says old data costs money to store and turns into a risk once it outlives its legal purpose.

How

Agility at Scale gives the roles: data owners decide for their own areas, data stewards enforce policy day to day, and data architects make sure the systems support it. Review policies regularly; programs run once go out of date within a year.

Epiq says retention policy must also cover what AI tools generate. The research found no retention schedules for models, prompts, embeddings or inference logs.

§10.2

Retention in Splunk: a worked example

You are hereStandard
  • §10.2.1
    An index's life

    Data is indexed and made searchable, stored and used, aged through hot, warm, cold and possibly frozen, then archived or deleted. §10.2.1

  • §10.2.2
    Seven steps

    Requirements, categories, periods, how buckets roll, automatic archival, testing, and communication and documentation. §10.2.2

  • §10.2.3
    Checking what is used

    An audit search shows which indexes people actually search, leaving out system searches. §10.2.3

  • §10.2.4
    An example configuration

    Hot for at most 24 hours, warm 30 days, cold 30 days, then frozen and archived. The page's note says "30 days" for a setting that actually counts buckets, so the master flags it. §10.2.4

  • §10.2.5
    The settings

    Size limits, the frozen time period, archive directories and scripts, and index reduction. §10.2.5

Who

IT carries it out, data owners define it, legal assures compliance. §10.2.6a

Rules

Every change is documented with its reason, the people involved and the date. §10.2.6b

Tools

Lifecycle policies that automate retention and deletion by category; alerts as data nears its age limit; regular age reports and reviews. §10.2.6c

What breaks

If no archive directory is set, frozen data is deleted by default. Measures: disk use, archiving time and load, search speed, and checksum matches. §10.2.6d

§10.3

Automating retention by policy

You are hereStandard
  • §10.3.1
    Why automate

    Varonis points to petabytes across systems, changing privacy rules, stale data, migrations and data kept in the wrong places. §10.3.1

  • §10.3.2
    What a policy keys on

Rules

Personal data kept past its permitted time is moved somewhere secure; exposed GDPR data is quarantined at once. §10.3.5b

No-code policies inside Varonis's platform. §10.3.5c

The pages say nothing about approval timeouts, rollback, misidentification or measures beyond the schedule options. §10.3.5d

Archived and active data mixed up; script errors and corruption; duplicate archives. §10.4.7d

06

Analysis

§7.0OverviewStandardExpert
You are here

Analysis uses tools and techniques to find patterns, trends and connections in data, and turns it into insight for business decisions. §7.0

In the journey · Stage 6Watch this stage

Part 1 of 6Where the data starts to answer.

Analysis turns data into insight with four questions: what happened, why, what may happen, and what to do. Tamsworth Health asks them of its governed Silver rows.

What

Turn governed data into answers

Analysis uses tools and techniques to find patterns, trends and connections in data, and draws out insight for decisions. Analysts do most of it and rely on data scientists for machine learning. Business stakeholders ask the questions and share the goals.

Tools: Analytical tools, such as Tableau or Power BI.

Owner: Analysts, Data scientists, Business stakeholders

How

Ask four questions

Four kinds of analysis answer four questions. Descriptive: what happened. Diagnostic: why. Predictive: what may happen. Prescriptive: the best thing to do within the limits that apply. Tamsworth asks all four about one goal: whether patients wait too long.

Tools: Statistical models, data mining, machine learning and optimization.

Owner: Analysts, Data scientists

Why

So every answer can be trusted

Every number should trace back to its source, so anyone can see how it was made. Who may use data, and for what purpose, is controlled too. Tamsworth's trace runs from each answer back through Stages 5 to 1, to the rows it began as.

Tools: Lineage tools, such as Apache Atlas.

Owner: Analysts

When

When a stakeholder brings a goal

Analysis starts from a question the business needs answered. At Tamsworth the goal comes from business stakeholders: are patients waiting too long? Stage 5 has already described the rows and set who may read them, so analysts can start at once.

Owner: Business stakeholders, Analysts

Next

Part 2: what happened

The first question is the simplest: what happened?

Owner: Analysts

Part 2 of 6What happened.

Descriptive analysis asks what happened. Tamsworth's analysts shape the Silver rows into a Gold table for one question, how long patients waited, and average it by month.

What

Summarize what happened

Descriptive analysis says what happened, in summaries and trends: a sales report, website traffic, who the customers are. At Tamsworth, analysts first shape the Silver rows into a Gold table made for one question: how long patients waited, by clinic and by month.

Owner: Analysts

How

Explore, then count and compare

Exploratory analysis looks at the data first, for patterns, outliers and problems. Then totals, averages and counts say what happened. Tamsworth works out each wait from the lab and survey parts of a row, and averages the waits by month: 34 minutes in November, against 28 in October.

Tools: Analytical tools, such as Tableau or Power BI.

Owner: Analysts

Why

Agree on what happened first

At Tamsworth the later questions stand on this one. Nobody can ask why the wait rose, or what to do about it, until it is clear that it rose: November's 34 minutes is above the expected range of 24 to 32.

Owner: Analysts

When

Every reporting cycle

Tamsworth's analysts read the rows each month for the report. Stage 5's audit log records that read: an analyst, with the sensitive fields hidden, for the monthly report. Reads are logged because who may use data, and for what purpose, is controlled.

Tools: Audit logs.

Owner: Analysts

Next

Part 3: why it happened

November's wait is above the expected range. The next question is why.

Owner: Analysts

Part 3 of 6Why it happened.

Diagnostic analysis asks why. Tamsworth's analysts split November's wait by clinic, then read what patients wrote in the survey.

What

Find the cause

Diagnostic analysis asks why something happened. It drills down, mines the data and builds statistical models; finding fraud and explaining why customers leave are examples. At Tamsworth, November's wait is above the range, so analysts look for the cause.

Owner: Analysts

How

Split it, then read what patients said

Tamsworth's analysts split November's wait by clinic. Clinic B waited 45 minutes; Clinics A and C about 28. Then they read Clinic B's survey comments, and three of them mention slow lab results.

Tools: Analytical tools that drill down, such as Tableau or Power BI.

Owner: Analysts

Why

A cause points to a fix

Knowing what happened is not enough to act on. At Tamsworth a cause points to a fix rather than a guess, so an analyst confirms it before anyone relies on it.

Owner: Analysts

When

When a result is out of range

Tamsworth looks for a cause when a result falls outside its expected range, as November's did. A result inside the range needs no diagnosis.

Owner: Analysts

Next

Part 4: one definition

Before anyone looks ahead, every report must count the wait the same way.

Owner: Analysts

Part 4 of 6One definition of every number.

A shared report should carry the definition of every number it shows. At Tamsworth Health, “wait” can be counted two ways, and two reports disagree.

What

Define each number once

Every number should trace back to its source, and a shared report should carry the definition of each number it shows. At Tamsworth, data stewards publish one definition of “wait”, and analysts use it.

Tools: Data catalogs that hold metric definitions; reports and dashboards with the definitions written in.

Owner: Analysts

How

Spot the conflict, publish one

At Tamsworth “wait” can be counted from check-in to seeing a clinician, or from check-in to leaving. The monthly report says 34 minutes; a dashboard says 52. A data steward publishes one definition, version 1, and both reports then show 34.

Owner: Analysts

Why

So people keep trusting the numbers

When two of Tamsworth's reports disagree about the same thing, people stop trusting both. With one definition, any answer can say how it was calculated.

Owner: Analysts, Business stakeholders

When

When a number changes or reports disagree

At Tamsworth a definition is written when a number is first created, and looked at again when it changes, or when two reports show different figures.

Owner: Analysts

Next

Part 5: what may happen

With a clear past, a cause and one definition, data scientists can look ahead.

Owner: Data scientists

Part 5 of 6What may happen.

Predictive analysis says what may happen. At Tamsworth Health, data scientists train a model on past rows to forecast December's wait.

What

Look ahead

Predictive analysis says what may happen, with statistical models, machine learning and data mining; credit risk and demand forecasts are examples. Data scientists own it. At Tamsworth, a model learns from past rows to forecast December's wait.

Tools: Machine learning and statistical models.

Owner: Data scientists

How

Learn, tune, test, forecast

Tamsworth's data scientists teach the model on most past rows, tune it on some, and hide the rest from it to test it. It forecasts about 41 minutes for December, for all three clinics together, give or take 4, if nothing changes.

Tools: Machine learning.

Owner: Data scientists

Why

Act before patients wait

A forecast lets Tamsworth act early. Testing on rows the model never saw shows how far to trust it: its forecasts land within 3 minutes. It is a likely outcome, not a promise.

Owner: Data scientists

When

Once the past is clear, then every month

Tamsworth forecasts once the past and the cause are clear. Each month it checks the forecast against the real wait, and retrains the model when the forecasts slip.

Tools: Machine learning.

Owner: Data scientists

Next

Part 6: what to do

A forecast says what is coming. The last question is what to do about it.

Owner: Data scientists

Part 6 of 6What to do.

Prescriptive analysis recommends the best action. At Tamsworth Health, the forecast misses the goal, so data scientists weigh three options, and a person decides.

What

Recommend an action

Prescriptive analysis finds the best course of action within the limits that apply, with optimization and decision science; stock levels and supply chains are examples. Data scientists own it, and business stakeholders set the goal.

Tools: Optimization and decision models.

Owner: Data scientists, Business stakeholders

How

Compare the options with the goal

Tamsworth's goal is a wait of 24 to 32 minutes. The model compares three options for December, for all three clinics together: faster lab results at Clinic B brings the wait to 33 minutes, more front-desk staff to 38, and doing nothing leaves it at 41.

Tools: Optimization and decision models.

Owner: Data scientists

Why

A person decides

The first three answers describe, explain and forecast. This one recommends an action, so a person keeps the decision: people keep control of key decisions, and the model only recommends.

Owner: Data scientists, Business stakeholders

When

When a forecast misses the goal

At Tamsworth it starts when a forecast misses a goal the business has set, as December's 41 minutes misses 24 to 32.

Owner: Business stakeholders, Data scientists

Next

Visualization

The answers go on to visualization, where they are shown in pictures and delivered to the people who must act on them.

Owner: Data scientists, Business analysts

With AIAct 2 · from the AI research file, not the master

Where AI can take the load

AI can take on much of the analysis itself: finding patterns and trends, predicting outcomes, recommending next steps, and answering questions people ask in plain words. Databricks says models can run all the time, so forecasting no longer waits for a scheduled report.

Why

Databricks lists faster analysis, better pattern finding, analysis opened up to anyone who can ask a question, and insight at scale. Informatica says business users lean on IT to find and understand data, which slows every answer down.

The research finds no measured gain for this stage. One data leader, speaking to CIO.com, says working with AI's query results means living with the fact that they are "not 100% certain".

How

DataHub says that in analytics a person usually sits between bad data and what it causes, while in AI systems that person is often absent, and no new checkpoint has been prescribed. Teradata says people set the objectives, check the outputs and make the final decisions; Databricks says relying on AI alone for analysis "is not" acceptable.

§7.1

The four types of analysis

You are hereStandard
  • §7.1.1
    Descriptive

    What happened: summaries and trends, such as sales reports, website traffic or who the customers are. §7.1.1

  • §7.1.2
    Diagnostic

    Why it happened: drilling down, data mining and statistical modelling, used for example to detect fraud, diagnose a system failure or explain why customers leave. §7.1.2

  • §7.1.3
    Predictive

    What may happen: statistical models, machine learning and data mining, used for example for credit risk, demand forecasts and personalized marketing. §7.1.3

  • §7.1.4
    Prescriptive

    The best course of action within the limits that apply: advanced algorithms, optimization and decision science, used for example to manage stock, supply chains and investment portfolios. §7.1.4

  • §7.1.5
    Exploratory analysis

    Looking at the data, and picturing it, to find patterns, relationships, outliers and problems before more advanced techniques are used. The other methods named are statistical modelling, algorithms, AI, data mining and machine learning. §7.1.5

Who

In KNIME's account, data analysts do most of the analysis and rely on data scientists for machine learning; data scientists handle prediction and prescription; business stakeholders ask the questions and share the goals; database governance teams set policies and standards. HBS says business analysts, data analysts or data scientists, depending on the problem and the size of the team. §7.1.6a

Rules

Splunk: watch how data is actually used, to confirm it stays within the standards and within legal and ethical limits. §7.1.6b

Tools

Language processing, machine learning and generative models find patterns, predict outcomes and generate insight at scale; agentic AI explores data on its own and recommends insights that fit the goals (KNIME). Analytical tools include Tableau and Power BI. Splunk names Hadoop, Apache Spark, Python and JavaScript in its processing stage. §7.1.6c

What breaks

Problems in the data, which exploratory analysis brings to light (HBS). KNIME states no risks for the analysis stage. §7.1.6d

With AIAct 2 · from the AI research file, not the master

Where AI can take the load

Teradata names an AI use for each kind of question: forecasting over time, such as churn or equipment failure; optimization models that recommend the next best action within a budget, capacity or policy; and reading emails, call transcripts and notes for names, sentiment and topics, as one healthcare system did with clinical notes to find gaps in care.

Domo says predictive analytics finds emerging trends and prescriptive models recommend next steps.

Why

AvePoint says lifecycle discipline means models learn only from current, authoritative data. Agility at Scale says clean, lifecycle-managed data speeds up analysts and data scientists.

How

Teradata's rule of thumb: start with the simplest technique that is accurate and explainable enough, then improve it. Its guardrails: for prediction, a held-back test set, a retraining schedule and watching performance; for prescription, writing the limits down accurately and simulating before going live; for health data, strict privacy controls and checking that models are fair across demographic groups.

Teradata warns of data leaking into a model's training and of a model's world drifting away from what it learned. Databricks warns that AI answers quickly and confidently, so people may trust it without checking.

§7.2

Real-time analysis

You are hereStandard
  • §7.2.1
    What it is

    Processing data as it is made and delivering insight as soon as events happen. Affordable cloud computing and fast frameworks brought it to the fore. §7.2.1

  • §7.2.2
    Core ideas

    Events are data points from users' actions or from the outside world, such as a price change. The processing may be a query, an algorithm or a model; joining live data with a large history makes the systems harder to run. Delay has two parts: from the event until the data can be processed, and from its arrival until the insight. §7.2.2a-c

  • §7.2.3
    Real time against batch

    Real time is set off by events; batch runs on a timetable, with results in hours or days, and makes better use of machines, throughput, compression and storage. Small batches are common. §7.2.3

  • §7.2.4
    Uses

    Real-time business intelligence serves managers and analysts, from simple alerts to short-window totals set against history. User-facing analysis sends insight straight to the people using a product, possibly millions at once, who can change a report's settings, so it needs more computing power. §7.2.4a-b

  • §7.2.5
    What it is built from

    A streaming platform takes in and holds fast-moving data: Apache Kafka or Redpanda, or cloud services such as AWS Kinesis, Azure Stream and Google Dataflow. A real-time analytics database joins new data with history: Apache Pinot, Apache Druid or ClickHouse. AWS Redshift and Azure Synapse have real-time features, which the source calls expensive in practice. §7.2.5a-b

  • §7.2.6
    Choices to weigh

    How fast the answer must be for the use; whether the streaming platform alone will do or a real-time database is needed; which platform and database; and how to run them: on your own machines, fully managed, or managed inside your own cloud account. §7.2.6

Who

Not stated in the master’s sources. §7.2.7a

Rules

Not stated in the master’s sources. §7.2.7b

Tools

A streaming platform plus a real-time database (see §7.2.5). The source gives no serving layers and no figures for how fast it must be. §7.2.7c

What breaks

Delay, of the data and of the processing, is the one measure stated. What goes wrong is not covered. §7.2.7d

§7.3

Sharing and use

You are hereStandard
  • §7.3.1
    Use as a stage

    Varonis treats use as a stage of its own: people in the organization classify, use and share data, and it may be made available to people outside. §7.3.1

  • §7.3.2
    Sharing as a stage

    Splunk treats sharing as a stage, to track how data is really used and confirm it follows business rules and standards. It names four kinds of data shared: operational data, master data, metadata and data users create. It lists productivity, lower upkeep, working together and better decisions as gains; the challenge is keeping shared data secure and compliant. §7.3.2

Who

People in the organization and, sometimes, outside parties (Varonis). Splunk does not otherwise address roles. §7.3.3a

Rules

Governance policies balance sharing against privacy (Splunk); the rules that apply are followed while data is in use (Varonis). §7.3.3b

Tools

Tracking systems and audit trails (Varonis), and Varonis's own automated classification, labelling and repair of permissions. §7.3.3c

What breaks

Insecure or non-compliant sharing (Splunk). Changes nobody logged, and data too widely available, which has to be contained (Varonis). §7.3.3d

§7.4

Keeping analysis running well

You are hereStandard
  • §7.4.1
    Good practice

    Run the stages of a pipeline on separate clusters or machines; keep watching and tuning processor, memory, disk and network use; adjust batch size, the number of machines and how the data is split. §7.4.1

  • §7.4.2
    Tuning a pipeline

    Simplify its logic, manage what it holds between steps, give it the right resources and settings, and split the data sensibly. §7.4.2

Who

Not stated in the master’s sources. §7.4.3a

Rules

Not stated in the master’s sources. §7.4.3b

Tools

Monitoring and logging find problems in the data and guide decisions about scale. §7.4.3c

What breaks

Processor, memory, disk and network use are the measures named for running it. §7.4.3d

§7.5

Controls on use and sharing

You are hereStandard
  • §7.5.1
    Who may use data, and why

    IBM: lifecycle management defines who may use data and for what purpose. Its methods are exploratory analysis, visualization, data mining and machine learning. Use inside covers daily work, workflows, dashboards and presentations; use outside covers service providers, for marketing analysis and advertising, for example. §7.5.1

  • §7.5.2
    Questions to ask

    Is the data encrypted? What metadata would make it easier to use? How is access managed for each type of data? Is it organized so it is easy to find and work with? How is it kept intact when someone changes critical data by mistake? §7.5.2

  • §7.5.3
    Finding, certifying and watching use

    Catalogs help people find data, certify it as fit to use, and watch how it is used (see §6.11.1). §7.5.3

  • §7.5.4
    Sharing and access practice

    Access by role or by attribute, masking, tokens in place of sensitive values, and audit logs (see §6.13.1). §7.5.4

Who

Not stated by two of its sources. Steward and owner roles are given under governance (§6.14). §7.5.5a

Rules

Lifecycle management defines who may use data and for what purpose (IBM). Use is restricted, and needs approval. §7.5.5b

Tools

Catalogs that watch how data is used. §7.5.5c

What breaks

People changing critical data by mistake. §7.5.5d

With AIAct 2 · from the AI research file, not the master

Where AI can take the load

AI can help data be analysed and shared without exposing the people in it: differential privacy, federated learning, where models train where the data sits, and anonymization. TierPoint and AngelHack also describe synthetic data, made by AI to resemble real data, for training models without real people's records.

Why

DATAVERSITY says using the same data across several AI systems is a compliance risk as well as a privacy problem. Teradata says sensitive data must be kept out of the prompts people type.

How

Agility at Scale says sharing and access controls decide who can use processed outputs, and on what terms. Splunk describes access by role, so only authorized people reach sensitive data. OvalEdge describes approval workflows for using sensitive data as a human gate, with automation handling routine requests inside the rules people set.

§7.6

Use, sharing and putting insight to work

You are hereStandard
  • §7.6.1
    Use against its purpose

    BigID: keep checking whether data is still used for the purpose it was approved for, because "existence does not justify continued appropriateness." It names uses from analytics and reporting to AI, automation and decisions. The master calls the failure use drifting from its approved purpose. §7.6.1

  • §7.6.2
    Examples of use

    Compyl's examples include tracking compliance by department, anticipating stock from ordering patterns, finding bottlenecks in production and sharing live risk data between departments. It calls use the stage where most of the lifecycle should happen, with workflows sending audit reports, security logs and sales leads to the right people. §7.6.2

  • §7.6.3
    The most sensitive phase

    Nutanix describes active data being read, processed and changed, under policies on who may reach it and why, for analysis, reporting, machine learning and sharing with partners. It calls this often the most sensitive phase, needing audit trails and tracking. §7.6.3

  • §7.6.4
    Ways to share

    Direct database access with row-level security, masked columns and role policies; data services through APIs, with limits, sign-in and documented schemas; scheduled reports and dashboards with their metric definitions written in; and data marketplaces with searchable catalogs and usage policies. Documentation covers what each field means, how often it updates, its limits and example uses. Governed APIs or scheduled syncs replace files sent by email. §7.6.4

  • §7.6.5
    Analysis and putting it to work

    The four types of analysis again; real-time analysis for detecting fraud and personalizing what people see; and activation, which pushes insight into the systems people work in. §7.6.5

Who

Not stated by two of its sources. BigID names owners and stewards (§6.14.4). §7.6.6a

Rules

Policies on access and purpose (Nutanix, BigID), and usage policies in data marketplaces. §7.6.6b

Tools

Governed APIs, scheduled syncs and automated workflows. §7.6.6c

What breaks

Use drifting from its approved purpose (BigID). In this sensitive phase, audit trails are required (Nutanix). §7.6.6d

With AIAct 2 · from the AI research file, not the master

Where AI can take the load

Analytics8 describes analytical agents that investigate a number in several steps: finding its sources, running the statistics and drafting first insights, sometimes split between a preparation agent, an analysis agent and a picture-making agent.

Why

A data leader, speaking to CIO.com, says terms used inconsistently lead AI to read the same data differently, and that changes decisions. Analytics8 adds that a foundation model can give different answers to the same question on the same data.

How

DataHub says to give agents explicit context a machine can read: what a number means, how fresh it is, who owns it, and whether it is approved for the use in hand. Teradata says plain-language queries need a semantic layer and access controls, checks on the queries AI writes, and logs of prompts and outputs.

07

Visualization

§8.0OverviewStandardExpert
You are here

Visualization shows information in pictures that make data understandable and communicate analysis quickly; serving delivers data to the people, apps and processes that use it. §8.0

In the journey · Stage 7Watch this stage

Part 1 of 5Make the answer visible.

Visualization turns results into pictures that are quick to understand, and delivers them to people who need them. At Tamsworth Health, each of Stage 6’s answers gets a chart.

What

Show results so people can act

Visualization is a picture of information that makes data understandable and communicates analysis quickly. Serving is the delivery: data reaches the people, apps and processes that need it, on time and reliably. Data scientists build the pictures, and business analysts present them.

Tools: Dashboard and report tools, such as Power BI or Tableau.

Owner: Data scientists, Business analysts

How

Choose a chart for the question

Pictures are chosen for the data and for the story to tell, with the audience and the goal in mind. Tamsworth gives each question its own chart: a number for how much, a line for how it is changing, bars for which clinic, and a line against a limit for when to act.

Tools: Dashboard and report tools, such as Power BI or Tableau.

Owner: Data scientists

Why

A picture is read at a glance

A picture communicates analysis faster than the rows behind it. Visualization is not strictly needed for every project, but it is increasingly important. Tamsworth’s answers go to one reader, the operations director, who decides where to send help.

Owner: Business analysts

When

Once there is an answer to show

The stage starts when analysis has answers that people must act on. Analysts often chart earlier too, while they explore the data. At Tamsworth, Stage 6’s answers are ready.

Owner: Data scientists, Business analysts

Next

Part 2: the dashboard

The charts come together in one view, built for its reader.

Owner: Data scientists, Business analysts

Part 2 of 5One view for the reader.

A dashboard puts the key numbers in one view for its reader. Data scientists build it, and business analysts present it. Tamsworth’s reads from Gold.

What

One view for the reader

A dashboard is one of the main forms of visualization, and it can be interactive or real-time. Tamsworth’s brings its key numbers and two charts together for the operations director, and reads from Gold, the table Stage 6 made for one question.

Tools: Dashboard tools, such as Power BI or Tableau.

Owner: Data scientists

How

Key numbers first, then the detail

A report starts from the key measures that matter most, its goal and its audience, then the measures of success, then a picture for each kind of data. Tamsworth puts four numbers across the top, and a trend and a split by clinic below.

Tools: Dashboard tools, such as Power BI or Tableau.

Owner: Data scientists

Why

Each number means one thing

A shared report or dashboard should carry the definition of every number it shows. Tamsworth’s 34 uses Stage 6’s one definition of “wait”, check-in to seeing a clinician, so it matches every other report.

Owner: Business analysts

When

When the reader opens it

A dashboard can be real-time. Tamsworth’s operations director opens this one when deciding where to send help.

Owner: Business analysts

Next

Part 3: trace a number

A reader who sees 34 minutes can ask where it came from.

Owner: Business analysts

Part 3 of 5Follow any number back.

Every number should trace back to its source. At Tamsworth Health, the operations director follows 34 minutes back to its rows.

What

Follow any number back

Every number should trace back to its source, with the logic that made it written down. At Tamsworth, a reader can follow 34 minutes from the dashboard to Gold, to the Silver rows, and to the rows collected in Stages 1 and 2.

Tools: Lineage tools, such as Apache Atlas.

Owner: Data stewards

How

Click, then walk back

Tamsworth’s operations director clicks the 34 and sees its path: the Gold table it reads from, the governed Silver rows, and their source. Stage 5’s trace already records each step.

Tools: Lineage tools, such as Apache Atlas.

Owner: Data stewards

Why

Check before acting

At Tamsworth, the operations director checks where a number came from before acting on it. The rule that every number traces back is set where data is processed; the sources give no lineage rule for visualization itself.

Owner: Business analysts

When

Whenever a reader questions a number

At Tamsworth the path is there whenever someone questions a figure. Each look is written to Stage 5’s audit log: who read the data, when and how.

Tools: Audit logs.

Owner: Data stewards

Next

Part 4: gate against no gate

The path shows where a number came from. Next: what the quality gate keeps out of it.

Owner: Data engineers

Part 4 of 5What the gate protects.

Quality rules are applied as data is processed, not after. Tamsworth charts November twice: with the rows that failed Stage 3’s quality gate, and without them.

What

Test rows before they are charted

Quality rules are applied while data is processed, not after, and validation checks that the output meets its standards. At Tamsworth, Stage 3’s quality gate tests every row; a row that fails waits in a repair queue instead of reaching a chart.

Tools: Data quality tools that test rows, such as Great Expectations, scheduled by Apache Airflow.

Owner: Data engineers

How

Same month, two charts

Tamsworth charts November twice from the same rows. Counted with the 6 rows that failed the gate, the wait reads 58 minutes. With them held back, it reads 34.

Owner: Data scientists

Why

A wrong number sends help the wrong way

At Tamsworth, 58 minutes would make November look like a crisis and send help where none is needed. The sources state no failure modes for visualization; failed validation is named where data is processed.

Owner: Data engineers

When

Every time rows arrive

At Tamsworth the gate tests every row before it can reach a dashboard, and a person works through the repair queue. Stage 3 showed one row failing; over November, six did.

Owner: Data engineers, A person

Next

Part 5: keep it current

A trusted number goes out of date. Next: an alert that tells people when a number crosses its limit.

Owner: Data scientists, Business analysts

Part 5 of 5Keep it current.

Dashboards can be real-time, and alerts fire when a number crosses a limit. Tamsworth sets one on each clinic’s weekly wait.

What

Keep the picture current

Dashboards can be real-time, and alerts can fire when a number crosses a set limit. Tamsworth’s rule: when a clinic’s weekly wait passes 32 minutes, tell that clinic’s lead.

Tools: Dashboard and monitoring tools with alerts, such as Grafana.

Owner: Data scientists

How

A limit, a crossing, an alert

Each week adds a point to Clinic B’s line. In November’s first week it reaches 33 minutes, past the limit of 32, and the alert goes to the Clinic B lead and into Stage 5’s audit log.

Tools: Dashboard and monitoring tools with alerts, such as Grafana.

Owner: Data scientists

Why

Before the month is over

The monthly report shows Clinic B’s November at 45 minutes only once the month is over. At Tamsworth, the alert reached the Clinic B lead in the month’s first week, while there was still time to act.

Owner: Business analysts

When

When a number crosses its limit

People set the rule and who is told; the alert fires when the limit is crossed. How often a dashboard should refresh is not stated in the sources, beyond real-time dashboards.

Owner: Data scientists, Business analysts

Next

Interpretation

The dashboard and the alert go on to interpretation, where people make sense of them, decide what to do, and act.

Owner: Business analysts, Business stakeholders, Executives

With AIAct 2 · from the AI research file, not the master

Where AI can take the load

AI can make the pictures itself. Databricks says AI creates charts, dashboards and summaries, and lets people ask questions in plain words and get explanations back; Teradata says it can generate dashboards with their written story and point out what changed. Both place visualization among the steps of analysis where AI takes part.

Why

Fivetran describes a faster path to insight, and Dremio a faster path from raw data to dashboards, reports and AI-driven results. Both are vendors.

How

Databricks says the right tool depends on the problem: forecasting needs strong predictive models, while dashboard work gains most from AI that makes the pictures. It also says the tools for this are merging into one suite, which is its own view as a vendor.

§8.1

Serving data to the people and systems that use it

You are hereStandard
  • §8.1.1
    Serving

    Delivering data to users, apps and the processes downstream, on time, reliably and accessibly. §8.1.1

  • §8.1.2
    Serving from a streaming pipeline

    The last step of a streaming pipeline: processed data goes to a store built for reading. The places named include databases, warehouses such as Google BigQuery, OpenSearch, data lakes, apps driven by events through Kafka, and other tools such as Elasticsearch, Splunk, Tableau and Datadog. §8.1.2

  • §8.1.3
    Who is served, and what they need

    Machine learning applications, often in large batches; data analytics; and business intelligence tools, which want data in real time. §8.1.3

Who

Not stated in the master’s sources. §8.1.4a

Rules

Not stated in the master’s sources. §8.1.4b

Tools

APIs; one source shows a REST endpoint as an example of something that reads the data. §8.1.4c

What breaks

Views that go stale, and the need for current data (see §8.4). §8.1.4d

§8.2

Kinds of picture, and building a report

You are hereStandard
  • §8.2.1
    Forms

    Charts and graphs; interactive and real-time dashboards; maps, such as heat maps and maps shaded by area; and more advanced pictures such as scatter plots, histograms and tree maps. §8.2.1a-d

  • §8.2.2
    Building a report

    Focus on the few measures that matter most; set the goals and know the audience; set the measures of success; choose a picture for each kind of data. Acceldata separates reporting, which presents information as text or tables, from visualization, which presents it as pictures. §8.2.2

  • §8.2.3
    Choosing the picture

    HBS: choose the picture for the data and for the story to tell. §8.2.3

Who

In KNIME's account, data scientists build visualizations of their models and check that they are accurate, and business analysts present the findings to stakeholders. §8.2.4a

Rules

Not stated in the master’s sources. §8.2.4b

Tools

KNIME: AI recommends or makes charts, dashboards and written summaries, and agentic AI watches how dashboards are used and how the data changes, then starts approved updates or alerts under rules set beforehand. Acceldata names Power BI and Tableau. §8.2.4c

What breaks

Acceldata brings in measures of a report's success but lists none. KNIME and HBS state no risks for this stage. §8.2.4d

Where AI can take the load

Analytics8 describes charts, the formulas behind them and written summaries made from a request in plain words, in Databricks AI/BI and Power BI.

Why

Analytics8 says pictures and summaries can come "in seconds". Kreate Technologies, writing on LinkedIn, calls cutting the time it takes to analyse data and act on it a competitive edge; the research rates that piece as opinion.

How

Teradata warns that generated output can be made up. Analytics8 says it can be hard to explain why an AI made a particular choice or recommendation.

§8.3

Reporting and business intelligence tools

Not stated in the master’s sources. §8.3.6a

Rules

Not stated in the master’s sources. §8.3.6b

§8.4

Keeping outputs current

  • §8.4.1
    Live dashboards and alerts

    Dashboards that update in real time, and alerts that fire when a number crosses a set limit. §8.4.1

    How often to refresh

    The sources do not say how often outputs should refresh, beyond real-time dashboards. §8.4.2

Not stated in the master’s sources. §8.4.3a

Rules

Not stated in the master’s sources. §8.4.3b

With AIAct 2 · from the AI research file, not the master

Where AI can take the load

Analytics8 describes workflows that watch business measures, write a summary in plain words of what changed, and send it by email or Teams.

Why

Databricks says quick summaries of large sets of data save hours of reading them by hand, and lists spotting the unusual in sensor readings, transactions and system logs among the jobs AI does.

How

Analytics8 expects that structured prompts may replace some dashboards and reports, or that the two will be used side by side.

08

Interpretation

§9.0OverviewStandardExpert
You are here

Interpretation makes sense of the analysis and the pictures, and uses them to make business decisions: people review, conclude, suggest an action and tell the story, and the end of the cycle feeds its beginning. §9.0, §9.1.1, §9.2.1

In the journey · Stage 8Watch this stage

Part 1 of 4Say what it means.

Interpretation turns analysis into decisions: it says what the numbers mean. Tamsworth starts from the Stage 7 dashboard.

What

Turn the dashboard into a decision

Interpretation makes sense of the analysis and the pictures, and uses them to make business decisions. Its work is to review the dashboards, draw conclusions, suggest actions, and present the findings as a story. Business analysts present; business stakeholders and executives decide.

Tools: Dashboard tools, such as Power BI or Tableau.

Owner: Business analysts, Executives

How

Review, then conclude

Dashboards, charts and graphs are reviewed for what they show. At Tamsworth, the analyst and the operations director find three things: November’s 34 minutes is above the 24 to 32 range, Clinic B is the worst at 45, and December is forecast at 41 for all three clinics.

Tools: Dashboard tools, such as Power BI or Tableau.

Owner: Business analysts

Why

Say what it implies

Interpretation explains what the data shows and what it implies: the weight is on implications, not only description. Tamsworth’s conclusion is one sentence: Clinic B drives the rise, and without action December misses the goal.

Owner: Business analysts

When

When a dashboard needs an answer

At Tamsworth, the dashboard shows a number above its range, and Stage 7’s alert has already reached the Clinic B lead. The sources state no rule for when interpretation starts.

Owner: Business analysts, Executives

Next

Part 2: weigh the options

A conclusion says what is wrong. Next: what could be done about it.

Owner: Business analysts

Part 2 of 4Weigh the options.

A conclusion leads to a suggested action. Tamsworth weighs three options for December: what each would change, and what it would cost.

What

Suggest an action

Interpretation suggests actions and gives strategic guidance. At Tamsworth, the three options come from Stage 6’s prescriptive answer, each with its forecast for December, all three clinics, and its cost.

Owner: Business analysts

How

Change and cost, side by side

Tamsworth’s options: faster lab results at Clinic B, about $6k a month, for 33 minutes in December; more front-desk staff, about $9k, for 38; or do nothing, for 41. None reaches the 24 to 32 goal; option 1 comes closest, 8 minutes better than doing nothing.

Tools: Dashboard tools, such as Power BI or Tableau.

Owner: Business analysts

Why

The weight is on what it implies

A forecast describes; a decision needs to know what each choice would change. At Tamsworth, the 8 minutes between doing nothing and option 1 is what the money would buy.

Owner: Business analysts, Executives

When

Before anything is committed

At Tamsworth the options are weighed after the conclusion and before any money or staff are committed. The sources give no rule or measure for this step.

Owner: Business analysts

Next

Part 3: tell the story

The options are weighed. Next: the analyst presents the choice, and a person decides.

Owner: Business analysts

Part 3 of 4Tell the story, then decide.

Business analysts present the findings as a story; executives decide. At Tamsworth, the analyst presents to the operations director.

What

Present, then decide

Findings are presented with storytelling. Business analysts present them; business stakeholders and executives make the decisions. People keep control of the key decisions.

Owner: Business analysts, Executives

How

One page, then a yes

Tamsworth’s analyst puts it on one page: what we saw, what we recommend, what to expect and what it costs. The operations director approves option 1, and the decision is written down.

Owner: Business analysts, Executives

Why

A person stands behind it

A person decides, and stands behind choices where accuracy matters. Governance, transparency and accountability matter more as AI takes part. At Tamsworth, a model could draft the story; the operations director owns the decision.

Owner: A person

When

When an option is ready

At Tamsworth, once the options are weighed and before any money or staff are committed. The sources state no policy for approvals at this step.

Owner: Executives

Next

Part 4: act and close the loop

Once a person says yes, the action has to happen, and the next month’s data shows whether it worked.

Owner: Executives

Part 4 of 4Act, then learn.

The final step feeds back into the first. At Tamsworth, the decision is carried out and watched.

What

Act, then feed it back

The lifecycle is a cycle: the final step feeds back into the first, and what one round teaches informs the next. Executives and business stakeholders take part in that loop.

Owner: Executives, Business stakeholders

How

Approved steps start

Agentic AI can start alerts, recommendations or workflows that were approved in advance; people keep the key decisions. At Tamsworth, an approved step asks the lab for faster results at Clinic B. Anything new goes back to a person.

Tools: AI agents that start only pre-approved steps.

Owner: Executives

Why

Watch, and ask again

At Tamsworth, Stage 7’s alert stays on Clinic B’s weekly wait. If the wait stays above 32, the alert reaches the Clinic B lead again and the options are reopened. The sources state no measure or failure mode for this loop.

Owner: Business analysts

When

After a yes, and every month after

The action starts once a person approves. At Tamsworth, each month’s new rows show whether it worked.

Owner: Executives, Business stakeholders

Next

Back to Stage 1

Next month’s rows are generated at the bedside, and the cycle starts again from Stage 1.

Owner: Executives, Business stakeholders

With AIAct 2 · from the AI research file, not the master

Where AI can take the load

AI can help people decide, not only read. Databricks describes a move from looking back at reports to looking ahead: spotting the unusual, forecasting risks and openings, and trying "what-if" scenarios; Teradata describes risk scores, forecasts and scenarios shaped to each role.

Why

Kreate Technologies, writing on LinkedIn, and Analytics8 say asking in plain words opens the numbers to people without deep SQL or chart skills; Analytics8 calls the aim a culture where insights are available to everyone, not just technical analysts.

How

Refonte Learning, a training provider writing as opinion, says people must be trained to read a model's results, know its limits and judge when to trust it, and that models work in service of human goals and under human direction.

§9.1

Interpretation: from the dashboard to a suggested action

You are hereStandard
  • §9.1.1
    What interpretation does

    KNIME lists four activities: review dashboards, charts and graphs for insights; draw conclusions about how the business is doing; suggest actions and strategic guidance, for example for marketing, product or customer engagement; and present the findings with storytelling. §9.1.1

  • §9.1.2
    What it implies

    HBS: apply expertise to explain what the data shows and what it implies. The weight is on implications, not only on description. §9.1.2

  • §9.1.3
    AI in interpretation

    KNIME: AI writes narrative explanations, summarizes insights and simulates outcomes; agentic AI triggers alerts, recommendations or workflows approved in advance. §9.1.3

Who

Business analysts present the findings; stakeholders and executives make the tactical decisions (KNIME). §9.1.4a

Rules

Not stated in the master’s sources. §9.1.4b

Tools

Nothing is named beyond the AI described above (§9.1.3); the sources name no tool for interpretation itself. §9.1.4c

What breaks

Not stated in the master’s sources. §9.1.4d

With AIAct 2 · from the AI research file, not the master

Where AI can take the load

CHI Software, a vendor, describes generative AI that reads dashboards, tables and reports and writes plain summaries for people who are not analysts, and names Power BI Copilot. Analytics8 describes chat assistants on analytics platforms that summarize dashboards, explain key numbers and answer follow-up questions.

An answer on ResearchGate, which the research rates as opinion, describes AI that reads dashboards or reports and sums up the trends, the unusual and the key numbers in plainer words.

Why

Analytics8 says automated workflows "reduce manual effort while keeping insights consistent".

How

Refonte Learning says a flood of AI-written content has to be checked before it is used.

§9.2

Feedback, and closing the loop

You are hereStandard
  • §9.2.1
    A cycle, not a line

    HBS: what one project teaches informs the next, and the final step feeds back into the first. §9.2.1

  • §9.2.2
    People keep the key decisions

    KNIME: feedback loops between people and AI mature, and people keep control of the key decisions. §9.2.2

  • §9.2.3
    Loops on the model side

    Machine learning is folded in to improve accuracy; real-time data keeps AI models current; AI and machine learning bring prediction, the spotting of the unusual and automated decisions; and AI's insights are only as good as the data under them. Model drift, retraining pipelines and evaluation sets are not covered by these sources. §9.2.3

Who

Executives and business stakeholders (KNIME). §9.2.4a

Rules

Governance, transparency and accountability (KNIME). §9.2.4b

Tools

AI agents running the work from end to end (KNIME). §9.2.4c

What breaks

Not stated in the master’s sources. §9.2.4d

With AIAct 2 · from the AI research file, not the master

Where AI can take the load

Teradata names acting as the last stage where AI takes part: it starts workflows, alerts and interventions, and puts its recommendations into the systems the business runs on.

Why

Teradata's table of benefits pairs live scoring and alerts on the unusual with risk and operations handled before problems grow.

How

Analytics8 says the work "should not rest entirely in the hands of AI": oversight is essential, agents should add to people's analysis rather than replace it, and each needs clear limits and uses.

§9.3

Running a use case (Splunk's framework)

You are hereStandard
  • §9.3.1
    Putting a use case in place

    Splunk's Success Framework sets out levels, from foundational to advanced: add-ons that bring data in; server classes for search, indexing, forwarding and collection; first requirements and naming rules; and a lab for testing and automation. §9.3.1

  • §9.3.2
    Telling people what changed

    In the same framework: tell those involved the work is done, announce it more widely, share the final showback figures with whoever asked, and track and report the business value to executive sponsors. §9.3.2

Who

Requesters, executive sponsors and budget owners (Splunk). §9.3.3a

Rules

Not stated in the master’s sources. §9.3.3b

Tools

Server classes, add-ons, the Add-on Builder and a lab environment (Splunk). §9.3.3c

What breaks

Splunk's stated measures are showback figures and the tracking of business value. §9.3.3d

Act 2

AI across the lifecycle

Overview
You are here

AI can do the routine first round of the work on data, but a person still signs off on anything costly or impossible to undo.

Stage and exact outline IDCore objective and primary data stateMetadata, cataloging and lineage requirementsSecurity, privacy and AI controlsStorage, infrastructure and automation triggersPrimary roles and ownershipCompliance frameworks, metrics and top failure modes
Planning§2.4 (also §2.3 design, planning and inventory)

Objective: set purpose, goals, consent and handling rules before data exists (§2.4.1, §2.4.3).

State: no data yet; plans, definitions, data management plans and an inventory of data types and locations (§2.4.2, §2.4.5).

Standardize lifecycle and definitions (§2.4.1). Tag at the source by origin, purpose, sensitivity, and by source and veracity (§2.3.2). Identify the system that owns the authoritative record (§2.4.3). Inventory of data types and locations (§2.4.5).

GDPR data minimization limits what is captured and how long it is kept (§2.4.1). Consent and permission checks (§2.4.3). Privacy and security policies set to match (§2.4.1). Question asked up front: should AI use this data (§2.4.4). Privacy controls list (§6.21.1).

Select collection and storage formats (§2.4.1). Audit current ecosystem and find shadow data (§2.3.1). No automation stated at this stage (§2.4.6).

Not stated for planning in the master's source; data management plans set ownership rules; owners and stewards defined elsewhere (§2.4.2, §6.14.4). Ownership per dataset assessed in the audit (§2.3.4).

Regulations: HIPAA, GDPR, PCI DSS and CMMC exposure from over-collection (§2.4.5, §6.7.6).

Failure: collecting data with no retention or deletion plan (§2.4.6); untagged, unvalidated ingestion starts quality problems (§2.3.4).

Generation§2.0 (pillars §2.1, §2.2)

Objective: data is created by systems, devices, people and algorithms (§2.1).

State: raw structured, unstructured or semi-structured data and events (§2.1.3, §2.1.4); captured at source, including change capture (§2.2).

Tag metadata at the source (§2.3.2). Event data carries a state change from a source system (§2.1.4). Retention requirements first appear at data onboarding (§2.1.5).

Synthetic data from generative models where real data raises privacy or compliance concerns (§2.1.1). Agentic AI can monitor new data against governance policies (§2.1.5).

Source systems: IoT, mobile apps, logs, message queues (§2.1.1). No capture automation stated (§2.2.3).

Data engineers build generation processes; IT staff maintain infrastructure (§2.1.5).

Failure: privacy and compliance exposure at creation (§2.1.5).

Metrics: none stated (§2.1.5).

Collection and ingestion§3.0

Objective: capture and move relevant data in without losing it (§3.1, §3.2).

State: raw data in motion and just landed; streams, batches, change events (§3.4, §3.5).

Request templates capture source hosts, path, access, retention requirement and volume (§3.1.3). Catalog holds sources, lineage and quality metrics at ingestion (§3.7.3). CDC change events kept as an audit log (§3.5.5). Schema-on-read and a canonical data model (§3.2.5, §3.4.7).

Encryption in transit and at rest; SASL, ACLs, TLS or mTLS; GDPR and HIPAA compliance; RBAC (§3.4.5, §3.4.7). Consent management and privacy automation are vendor features (§3.8.2). AI automates extraction; agentic AI decides what to collect (§3.1.4).

Push, pull and hybrid models; ETL, ELT, federation (§3.2.1, §3.2.2). Backpressure, retries, checkpointing (§3.4.7). Prefer log-based CDC (§3.5.6). Target 80% of sustained throughput; default retention 24 hours (§3.4.5).

Data engineers integrate sources; business stakeholders confirm needed data is collected (§3.1.4). No named role for streaming (§3.4.7).

Regulations: GDPR, HIPAA (§3.4.7); sharing agreements for third-party data (§3.7.5).

Metrics: throughput in MB/s or GB/s and latency (§3.4.5).

Failure: data loss from overload, out-of-order events, Kafka disk growth (§3.4.7); trigger-based CDC slows source writes (§3.5.6).

Processing and transformation§4.0

Objective: make data trustworthy and usable (§4.1).

State: cleaned, reshaped, integrated, validated data; batch or streamed (§4.1.1, §4.2, §4.3).

Documented transformation logic, versioned scripts, audit trails (§4.6.3). End-to-end lineage so every metric traces to its source; certify datasets (§4.6.4). Schema drift management (§6.4).

Encrypt sensitive data; scrub PII; tokenization, anonymization, pseudonymization (§4.7.1, §4.7.2). Compliance monitoring of data use (§4.1.5). ML cleaning and agentic pipeline monitoring (§4.1.5).

Orchestration and transformation tools (§4.4); batch and stream patterns (§4.2, §4.3); Lambda and Kappa (§4.4.5); checkpointing (§4.3.8). Pipeline architecture principles (§4.5.1).

Data engineers build ETL; data scientists explore raw data (§4.1.5). Ownership assigned before release (§4.6.8).

Regulations: GDPR, CCPA, HIPAA, PCI DSS, PIPEDA, DPA 2018, Australian Privacy Principles (§4.1.5).

Failure: duplicate spikes, schema changes, failed validation (§4.1.5); undocumented logic spreads errors (§4.6.8).

Storage§5.0

Objective: keep data accessible, protected and backed up (§5.0 definition).

State: stored in databases, warehouses, lakes, hubs or lakehouses (§5.1); hot, warm, cold or frozen (§5.4).

Lineage differs by architecture; lakes need metadata management to avoid a data swamp (§5.1.2, §5.1.3). Log of storage locations and data movements (§5.6.3). Naming protocol and document workflow (§5.7.1).

Protection matched to sensitivity; encryption at rest and in transit; key rotation; network segmentation (§5.3.2, §5.6.2). Immutable backup copy (§5.3.1). AI analyzes access patterns to recommend tiering (§5.1.9).

Tiering hot, warm, cold, archive (§5.6.4, §5.7.5). Splunk bucket rolls and settings (§5.4.2). Deduplication, compression, incremental backups (§5.7.3, §5.7.4). Load balancing, failover, DR (§5.7.7). RTO and RPO (§5.6.3).

Database administrators manage storage; IT and security ensure security and backup (§5.1.9).

Regulations: HIPAA technical safeguards, GDPR, SOX (§5.6.6).

Metrics: RTO, RPO (§5.6.7); users retain 2% of data year over year (cited, §5.7.10).

Failure: data swamp, backup failures, corruption, bloated backups (§5.1.9, §5.7.8).

Management and governance§6.0 (runs alongside all stages)

Objective: keep data accurate, private, trusted and usable throughout (§6.0 definition, §6.1).

State: applies to data in every state.

Metadata, catalog and lineage (§6.5); catalog role per stage and active metadata (§6.11); schema drift (§6.4); lineage coverage and freshness metrics (§6.18.1).

CIA triad (§6.20); security and access (§6.2); privacy controls and consent (§6.21); discovery and classification (§6.22); DLP and maintenance (§6.23); AI lifecycle controls (§6.24); AI-era risks (§6.9.1).

Policy as code with five policy categories (§6.12); ROT discovery and quarantine (§6.8); implementation methods (§6.15); tool landscape (§6.16).

Governance roles (§6.1.6); owners, stewards, council, deletion committee (§6.14); roles added later (§6.14.4).

Regulations: all named regulations (§6.7, §6.7.5, §6.7.6).

Metrics: §6.18.1, §6.18.5.

Failure: §6.17 (including §6.17.8 to §6.17.12).

Analysis and consumption§7.0

Objective: turn data into insight with four analytics types (§7.1).

State: governed data in active use; real-time or batch (§7.2, §7.3).

Catalog certification and usage monitoring (§6.11.1, §7.5.3). Every metric traceable to source (§4.6.4). Metric definitions embedded in shared reports (§7.6.4).

Who may use data and for what purpose (§7.5.1); RBAC or ABAC, masking, tokenization, audit logs (§6.13.1). Purpose drift tracked (§7.6.1). AI risk patterns for stale, duplicate and sensitive data (§6.24.2).

Real-time analytics database plus streaming platform (§7.2.5); cluster separation and tuning (§7.4); governed APIs and scheduled syncs (§7.6.4); activation into operational systems (§7.6.5).

Analysts, data scientists, stakeholders, governance teams (§7.1.6). Steward and owner roles (§6.14).

Metrics: data and processing latency (§7.2.7); CPU, memory, disk I/O, network (§7.4.3).

Failure: insecure sharing, unlogged alterations (§7.3.3); users unintentionally altering critical data (§7.5.5); use drifting from approved purpose (§7.6.6).

Visualization and serving§8.0

Objective: make results understandable and deliver them (§8.1, §8.2).

Not stated for visualization itself (§8.1.4, §8.3.6). Metric definitions embedded in shared reports are in §7.6.4.

Not stated at this stage (§8.1.4). AI recommends charts and narrative summaries; agentic AI triggers approved updates (§8.2.4). Sharing controls apply (§6.13).

BI and reporting tool categories (§8.3); alerts when thresholds are crossed (§8.4.3). Refresh cadence not specified beyond real-time dashboards (§8.4.2).

Data scientists build visualizations; business analysts present (§8.2.4).

Compliance: not stated (§8.2.4, §8.3.6).

Metrics: KPIs for report success, none listed (§8.2.4).

Failure: not stated (§8.3.6, §8.4.3).

State: analyzed and visualized data informing action.

Not stated (§9.1.4).

AI narratives and simulations; agentic AI triggers pre-approved workflows (§9.1.3). Humans keep control of key decisions (§6.9.5). Agents inherit stage of data they read (§6.19).

End-to-end orchestration by AI agents (§9.2.4). Use-case implementation and communication steps (§9.3).

Business analysts present; stakeholders and executives decide (§9.1.4). Executives and stakeholders in feedback loops (§9.2.4).

Retention and archival, including legal hold§10.0 (legal hold §10.6.2)

Objective: keep data as long as obligations and value require, then preserve what must not be deleted (§10.1, §10.6).

State: inactive, archived, frozen, quarantined or held (§10.4, §10.3.4, §10.6.2).

Retention windows mapped to classification (§10.1.3). Catalog of archived data, documented metadata, search (§10.4.3). Archived data indexed, non-alterable format (§10.4.1, §10.5.3). Audit-ready records of retention periods and access (§6.7.5).

Archive separated from active data (§10.4.2). Encrypted archives (§10.6.5). Legal hold blocks deletion while rules run elsewhere (§10.6.2). Integrity checks by checksum or hash (§10.4.6). Quarantine is reversible (§10.3.4).

Splunk hot, warm, cold, frozen settings and archive scripts (§10.2). Triggers: inactivity, retention policy, business events (§10.5.1). Policy attributes, schedules, stub files, approvals (§10.3). Archive in clusters (§10.4.5).

IT implements; legal and compliance set periods; data owners define; business units differ (§10.1.6). Legal teams named in BigID role list (§10.6.7).

Regulations: GDPR, HIPAA, PCI DSS (§10.1.1); regulatory variants of archive (§10.5.6).

Metrics: Splunk retention metrics (§10.2.6); datasets under hold; over-retained volume (§6.18.5).

Failure: over-retention (§6.17.10); unset archive directory means frozen data is deleted (§10.2.6); disconnected legal holds (§6.17.8).

Deletion, destruction and defensible deletion§11.0 (defensible deletion §11.7.2)

Objective: remove data securely and prove it (§11.1, §11.7).

State: quarantined, deleted, destroyed, or derived copies still to be traced (§11.3, §11.7.5).

Deletion log with locations and dates (§11.6.2). Timestamps, methods, verification records (§11.6.3). Immutable audit logs of when and why (§11.6.4). Lineage and lifecycle context to trace copies (§11.7.4).

Overwrite, destroy media or encrypt at rest (§11.2.3); cryptographic erasure (§11.6.3). Quarantine first (§11.3). Deletion in AI indexes, vector stores, derived datasets and caches (§11.4.2, §11.7.4, §6.24.2). Erasure on request (§11.4.1).

Automated deletion from retention policy (§11.6.4). Data subject requests across production, archive and backup (§6.7.5). Quarantine and stub files (§11.3.1). Retire use cases and their data (§11.5).

Data deletion committee (§6.14.1, §11.6.2). Customer decides after quarantine (§11.3.2). Approver and owner recorded per deletion (§11.7.7).

Regulations: GDPR erasure (§11.4.1); NIST SP 800-88 for regulated data (§11.6.4); GDPR and HIPAA drivers (§11.2.4).

Metrics: time from expiration to deletion; percentage of validated deletions (§6.18.5).

Failure: logical delete leaves data on disk (§11.2.4); manual deletion queues (§6.17.8); deletion not cascading to AI copies (§11.4.2).
